records.text: 22 May 2026 Focus Germany Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG the most significant spending outflows typically take place in November and December (see Figure 6). Investment spending dynamics On a 12-month trailing sum basis, total investment spending (core budget, SV IK) continued its visible rise in April, nearing EUR 99 bn (March: approximately EUR 92 bn; see Figure 7). Despite this ongoing upward trend, investments must still be significantly increased during the remainder of the year to meet the full-year 2026 target of about EUR 116 bn (approximately 2.5% of 2026F GDP). Breaking down the figures monthly, total investment expenditures climbed by about EUR 9.5 bn in April, up from the roughly EUR 6 bn seen in March (as depicted in Figure 8). A key driver of this acceleration was the SVIK's expenditure outflow, which quickened in April following a more subdued pace in February and March. Core budget investments, however, presented a different picture, increasing by just EUR 3 bn month-over-month, a relatively minor uptick when compared with the same period last year. On a ytd basis, aggregate investments have now amounted to approximately EUR 33 bn, marking a substantial increase of almost EUR 19 bn compared with April 2025. Consequently, approximately 28% of the government's expenditure target has thus far been attained (see Figure 12). This part of the story is already in play and will lead to more dispersion and more negative headlines, but it may not be enough on its own to tighten broader financial conditions. But an actual deterioration in software fundamentals is likely to be the catalyst that could meaningfully tighten financial conditions, as the US rating-agencies and third-party valuers assessing private credit fund portfolios quickly adjust their models. On the US rating agency side, actual evidence of slowing revenue growth, lower free cash flow generation, and/or reduced customer retention ratios will reduce the ability of many software companies to refinance upcoming maturity walls, that will need to be dealt with within 1-2 years. This would certainly increase rating agency downgrades. But if this fundamental pressure does emerge, the downgrade pressure on broader-spec grade credit could be significant. The challenges around the inflation forecast remain as they were at the time of the last GEOS: Hormuz; fiscal intervention on energy bills; degree of pass-through into second-round effects. records.text: CDS Relative Value UK corporate CDS: a cross-asset lens CDS on UK names have seen limited repricing recently despite rising political volatility, with risk premia noticeably below prior episodes. We assess CDS through a cross-asset lens relative to both cash and equity markets to identify dislocations in UK names. UK risk on wider end ahead of recent developments, little underperformance since UK politics came firmly into focus last week, with a leadership challenge to Keir Starmer becoming tangible with potential successors entering the contest. Against a backdrop of heightened fiscal uncertainty, this triggered a renewed sell-off in the rates market with both 10y and 30y gilt yields rising to multi-decade highs. In this context, the response in CDS for UK names has been contained. For non-financials, the UK versus broader non-financial basis has widened noticeably over a one-year horizon, with the differential now near the upper end of its range (dark-blue line, Figure 1). However, this largely reflects a widening since early April rather than an abrupt repricing more recently. Since 8 May, when gilts began selling off, UK CDS has widened less than 1bp, ie, while UK non-financial CDS screens stretched relative to non-UK peers, the impact of recent political volatility has so far been muted. records.text: eadcounts fall, spending optically steady but boosted by fuel Nominal growth in consumer spending was 1.7% y/y in the 4wks to 8 May. Yet the increased fuel spending amid rising prices masks the underlying picture, where most categories are decelerating/declining. In the labour market, both vacancies and headcounts are falling but perhaps less than expected. Consumer spending boosted by fuel spending, but underlying is weaker across many categories: Total spend increased +1.7% year-on-year (nominal growth) for the four weeks ending 8 May, which is optically in line with the pre-war trend of 1-1.5%. However, when considering the 18% y/y increase in fuel spending (compared to a contraction of 13-14% pre- war), and looking at individual category level spending, it is becoming clear that there is some underlying weakness in large segments of consumer spending. Travel spend in particular is the standout category that has seen a pronounced negative impact since the start of the Middle East conflict. Our alternative UK labour market data sources suggest declines in job vacancies and headcounts: Our shadow indicator for economy-wide headcounts, based on Revelio headcounts data, moved downwards slightly, though half the industries had headcount growth in the seasonally adjusted April data. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 27 Turkey Market focus centered on the April rate decision and the May Inflation Report (IR). As expected, the CBT kept its policy rate unchanged at 37% in the April MPC meeting. We believe that the CBT's decision to hold the policy rate rather than align it with the average funding rate signals a wait-and-see stance in the near-term. Turning to the May IR, the governor’s presentation was framed around one dominant theme: the supply shock from the Middle East conflict and the Strait of Hormuz closure. In our view, two signals stood out. First, the new forecasts assume policy stays tighter for longer than envisaged in the previous Report. Second, in a structural shift, the CBT will abandon forecast-band communication in favor of baseline point forecasts paired with a narrative risk assessment. Against this backdrop, we expect the CBT to keep rates on hold at the next MPC meeting, barring renewed pressures on reserves. Looking beyond June, we expect the room for easing in 2H to be more limited than the consensus view suggests, with the policy rate ending the year at 35%, versus the consensus of about 32%; if anything, the risks to our forecast are titled toward a tighter stance. However, this is not to imply that such an event has no consequence for the inflation market, as second-order distortions could emerge. For instance, if nominal USTs cheapen disproportionately to TIPS on the back of any Japanese repatriation flows, that would widen breakevens, all else equal. While directionally that is correct, that is only a partial equilibrium solution and likely would be missing out on more macro factors that would be influencing underlying inflation risk via tighter financial conditions and/or currency movements. Parsing through all the permutations there is beyond the scope of this section. Instead, perhaps a cleaner expression could be via tightening pressure on iotas (the breakeven widens relative to CPI swaps). records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 26 Czech Republic, Hungary, & Poland Czech Republic The Czech economy is forecast to grow by around 2.1% YoY this year despite the negative supply shock amid ongoing tensions in the Middle East, supported mainly by household consumption, real wage growth, and a gradual recovery in investment. The output gap should remain slightly negative this year and close only in 2027, when growth is expected to accelerate to 2.6% YoY. Headline inflation is projected at 2.4% YoY this year, driven mainly by higher energy and fuel prices and persistent core pressures in services, while temporarily overshooting 3% at the start of next year, when it should average 2.6% YoY. We continue to assume the CNB policy rate to remain at 3.50%, still acting as mildly restrictive, until potential second-round effects of the energy shock begin to materialize in core inflation, wages, and inflation expectations. Hungary Flash GDP estimates indicate that economic growth accelerated to 1.7% YoY in the first quarter. While a detailed breakdown is not yet available, we attribute this improvement partly to a boost in consumer demand, supported by accommodative fiscal policies and a one-off pre-election increase in public sector wages. The economic acceleration is accompanied by a better inflation outlook, as we expect inflation to stay below 3.5% by the end of the year. The subsidy amount, which started at JPY30.2 per liter, temporarily rose to just under JPY50 as market prices increased, before reaching JPY42.6 on 14 May. As of end-April, the balance of the fund that could be diverted to gasoline subsidies stood at JPY980bn, implying that if the subsidy remained at current levels, the fund would be exhausted by end-June. The additional budget required will naturally depend on the size and duration of the gasoline subsidy. For example, if the subsidy remains unchanged at JPY42.6 and continues through end- September, an additional JPY1.1trn would be required. If gasoline prices rise further, the subsidy expands to JPY60 and the program continues through end-October, more than JPY2trn in additional funding would be needed ( Figure 2). The government has budgeted JPY1trn in contingency reserves for FY26, but that alone may prove insufficient; even if not, there would still be a case for securing new budget funding for gasoline subsidies in order to prepare for unforeseen disasters going forward

The KR news came the same morning that Walmart reported in-line 1Q but highlighted a 250bp profit headwind from higher fuel and logistics. On Wednesday, it was reported Pepsi plans to raise prices on single-serve chips. This confluence led to questions about competition, inflation, price gaps and here, we briefly address a few of them. KR has already been narrowing price gaps Robby Ohmes’ most recent pricing study (April, Las Vegas), showed KR's price gap vs. WMT on a total food basket basis (60 items) has decreased from 14% in 2025 to 10% in 2026. The largest price gaps vs. WMT appear to be in Meat (25%), Dairy (14%), and Produce (7%). On Center Store, KR has maintained tighter spreads vs. WMT (2% in April). KR has rolled out price tests in select markets (with less competition) and plans to phase-in additional tests. We expect KR to reduce promotions while instituting more competitive EDLP spreads. Our optimistic “ quick resolution” scenario released in late March (see Geopolitics reshuffle world energy flows again )— with the assumption that full oil flows would be restored in Hormuz in short order — seems now highly unlikely. With a double -blockade now firmly in place, strait vessel crossings have failed to pick up for now. The physical oil market continues to tighten as a large share of global seaborne volumes remain trapped in the Middle East and gl obal oil markets remain in steep backwardation. A strait that is neither fully open nor totally closed in 2Q/3Q may push Brent to average $120/bbl this year. More adverse scenarios, including a resumption of military action, remain plausible too. A “renewed hostilities ” scenario that extends into the early summer could push Brent to average $150/bbl or more in 2026, a record. DSL-Bund: closing the gap This section is an excerpt from DSL-Bund: closing the gap, published 20 May Pre-pandemic, the Netherlands and Germany were both enjoying healthy growth, balanced budgets and downwards trends in debt/GDP ratios. Post-pandemic however, Germany has persistently lagged from a growth standpoint, fuelling structural fiscal pressures (a theme we previously discussed in detail in German ASW: A tale of the tightening). In contrast to Germany, the Netherlands has managed to keep pace with the broader eurozone in terms of growth, in part reflecting the country's lower reliance on structurally-challenged manufacturing industries. In that context, the post-pandemic deterioration of budget deficits has been much less stark for the Netherlands than for Germany. Hence, whereas German issuance volumes have ballooned in recent years, Dutch issuance volumes have remained relatively more contained. This backdrop of relatively healthier Dutch fundamentals versus a more structurally challenged picture for Germany appears set to continue for an extended period: IMF forecasts project significant Dutch growth/fiscal outperformance versus Germany from now through 2031. As such, Germany's debt/GDP ratio is projected to increase by c.9pp over the next five years to c.74%, versus Dutch debt/GDP increasing by only c.4pp to c.48% ( Figure 6). records.text: A Relatively Strong Fiscal Response to the Energy Crisis Leaves the Fiscal Balance in a Good Place Spain’s lower energy intensity helps contain the direct hit to growth, while fiscal risks remain manageable despite a relatively significant policy response. Since the 2022 energy crisis, Spain has been the least exposed in the EMU4 to the surge in energy prices. The fiscal cost of the most common measures used to shield consumers also sit at the lower end of the distribution in Spain, with the notable exception of tax cuts for petrol and diesel (Exhibit 3). However, Spain has delivered one of the most forceful energy-related fiscal responses in the region. Its decision not to prioritise defence spending and its relative insulation from the shock has allowed policymakers to provide support without materially undermining the broader fiscal position. records.text: 18 World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 SEK: our preferred de-escalation hedge Marcus Boman Michalis Rousakis MLI (UK) MLI (UK) Themes: a trade for the optimistically minded We are constructive SEK and recently went short EURSEK. SEK has lagged its high ‑beta peers, both since the start of the US/Iran war and following the ceasefire. While its underperformance during the active phase of the conflict did not surprise us, we would have expected a stronger rebound as tensions eased. As a result, we see meanin gful catch‑up potential in a peace ‑deal scenario. If de-escalaiton occurs, SEK also looks attractive from a macro perspective. We expect renewed USD weakness beyond the near term, continued support from Germany's fiscal push and European defence spending, and Sweden to deliver one of the strongest growth rates in G10 - partly supported by its own meaningful fiscal push ( Exhibit 39). Even under a more adverse scenario, we view downside risks as more contained than for other de-escalation trades. As an electricity exporter with a strong fiscal position, Sweden is better placed than most G10 peers to weather energy -related growth shocks. Revisiting the Outlook for the Fed’s Balance Sheet The Federal Reserve’s balance sheet policy and its footprint in financial markets have come back into focus since the selection of Kevin Warsh as the next Chair of the Federal Reserve. Warsh has been a long-time critic of the Fed’s asset purchase programs and large balance sheet, having opposed the Fed’s QE2 program before resigning from the Fed after it was announced. In his criticism, Warsh has noted that the Fed’s balance sheet remains far larger than it was before the 2008 financial crisis, continuing to call for its shrinking in the lead-up to his selection and during his confirmation hearing, and making the case that a smaller balance sheet would allow the Fed to lower the funds rate. Fed Governor Miran and Dallas Fed president Logan have recently discussed the ample reserves framework and options for reducing the size of the Fed’s balance sheet. Their assessment of the benefits of the current framework and the wider support within the FOMC suggest that an imminent change is unlikely. But the level of reserves that constitutes ample can evolve. A range of officials—including Governor Waller and SOMA Manager Perli, as well as Governor Miran and president Logan—have acknowledged that evidence of a reduction in reserve demand would warrant an adjustment in the supply of reserves. If AI ends up affecting all tasks, everything else equal, those productivity gains would multiply by more than 5. Alternatively, even if only 20% of tasks could be transformed by AI, if it becomes cost-effective to use AI with all of them, productivity gains in the next decade would multiply by more than 7. AI is different (2): the productivity of innovation More importantly, AI can also increase the productivity of innovation, i.e. it has the potential to affect cognitive work and the generation of ideas. In other words, it can make innovation more productive. This is key: the ability of AI to increase the productivity of innovation is what, in the long term, can make it go beyond a one-off level effect on productivity to impacting productivity growth. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 3 The global economy remains in the jaws of a severe supply shock due the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Roughly 10 million barrels a day of petroleum supply are currently offline, and the price of Brent oil is trading around $110/barrel. As such, we judge that the downside risks to economic activity and the upside risks to inflation remain acute. Even so, various real-time readings on global economic activity have continued to point to solid performance. This reflects the accelerating strength of AI spending. But more broadly, the global economy looks to be absorbing the oil shock fairly smoothly. Various dimensions of adjustment have been in play.1 These include a drawdown of global oil inventories and a shift to other fuel sources, as well as efforts to increase efficiency and, ultimately, “demand destruction” due to the direct effects of higher oil prices. Consistent with this view, the March and April readings of the global PMIs have held up surprisingly well (Figure 1). The services PMI has retreated a notch over this period, and it’s currently running near the lower end of its range in recent years. That said, it remains above 50, which signals that growth has continued. The global manufacturing PMI has actually moved up on balance over the last two months, posting its strongest readings in recent years. This reflects a mix of factors. Even if all output is eventually curtailed, it is plausible that the regime can survive for many months, even years, through money printing and other wartime measures, with the burden of national impoverishment likely falling on non-establishment linked society. records.text: key question for risk assets is not whether rates remain high, but how markets absorb them. For equities, the answer so far has been earnings. European Q1 earnings surprised positively, with EPS up 7% y/y – the strongest growth since 2022. This reinforces our equity strategists' simple but powerful conclusion: equity markets can live with higher rates as long as growth holds up and earnings are not materially impaired. Their key risk remains a growth slowdown that feeds through to weaker profitability. Higher rates affect credit through two main channels: fundamentals and demand. On fundamentals, as we discuss here, high yield stands out given the sizeable maturity wall in 2028-29. However, even assuming materially higher refinancing yields – 100bp for BBs and 150bp for Bs – interest coverage ratios remain comfortably above 2x for most issuers, provided earnings do not fall. As with equities, the implication is clear: absent a recession, higher rates are manageable from a financing perspective. That said, the higher rates go, the more sensitive credit becomes to economic downside: the compensation for taking cyclical risk and HY over IG risk should improve with higher rates. On the demand side, higher yields remain supportive, particularly for IG. In the current regime, fixed-maturity fund demand is structurally more important for IG, and yield targets are more easily met without dipping into HY. This dynamic continues to skew technicals in favour of IG over HY. 22 May 2026 3

records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 23 India Downward growth revision: With intensifying risk from El Nino and continued disruption at the SoH, we have cut our FY27 GDP growth forecast to 6.6% (from 7.1%), with most impact seen in 1HFY27. This revision stems from a combination of supply-side disruptions (sensitivity to higher oil prices, Petchem and other product disruptions, maritime disruptions), demand impacts (weaker exports, reduced non-energy consumption, El Nino's effect on rural demand), and potential second- round effects (weaker balance sheets, income growth, asset prices, and subdued sentiments). We foresee limited further space for demand-side fiscal stimulus, as there is already between 20-50bps of GDP fiscal slippage risk due to the conflict. Stable inflation forecast but rising risks: The April print and underlying drivers were largely in line with our forecast, and INR 3/liter fuel price hike was also close to our estimate (INR 5/liter). Consequently, we retain our base case headline inflation forecast at 4.6%YY average for FY27, consistent with RBI view. In our current forecast, inflation peaks at 5.4%YY in 3QFY27. We see core inflation at 4.4%YY in FY27. While our base case stays unchanged, the risk around this forecast is increasing and tilted to the upside (40-60bps) from higher oil prices and El Nino. records.text: s to be exercised in order to remain strong. “We have learned from experience that increases in money market rates to levels even modestly above IORB can become disruptive very quickly, with attendant consequences not only for rate control but also for the stability of repo markets and, by extension, the Treasury market. ” -SOMA Manager Perli Even so, the Fed is likely to move cautiously. Chair-Designate Warsh has suggested that any balance sheet changes would take time and be debated rigorously, so an abrupt about-face in the near term seems unlikely. Perli also pointed out that the results of the March SFOS show that the reserve demand curve is quite steep, meaning that should the Fed push into reserve scarcity, the pickup in funding pressures could be abrupt. This means that banks would need substantially higher overnight rates to induce them to shed even a modest amount of reserves. This key point reinforces their cautious approach to attempting to push reserves into the scarce zone, with Perli saying that “we have learned from experience that increases in money market rates to levels even modestly above IORB can become disruptive very quickly, with attendant consequences not only for rate control but also for the stability of repo markets and, by extension, the Treasury market. ” In other words, its a bad idea to risk blowing up the repo market in an attempt to shrink the balance sheet only modestly, and it is hard to disagree that the risk reward looks very asymmetric.

However, in our view, it is a question of when, not if, NOK strength reverses . If hopes for a peace deal materizlies, oil prices are likely to grind lower . In addition, some damage to global growth has probably already occurred, which could weigh on risk assets in the near term. We have previously argued that the only scenario in which NOK could strengthen further would be a combination of elevated energy prices without spillovers to global growth . This is the scenario that markets have priced since the start of the war. Expectations that a peace deal could come at any moment have kept concerns around global growth contained, while the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz has supported oil pric es. Looking ahead, however, we still struggle to justify NOK trading at current levels. A re - escalation of the war in Iran would likely send oil prices much higher and revive global growth concerns, rather than be treated as a pure terms ‑of‑trade shock, potentially weighing on NOK. records.text: suance We begin by stating the obvious: not every rise in gilt yields is a signal on UK fiscal policy. Indeed, the move in gilts – even after the local elections – coincided with moves in US Treasuries and German Bunds. The main question therefore is how much of the gilt sell-off was genuinely domestic in origin, and what that implies for the fiscal arithmetic markets are pricing. To answer this, we implement two steps. First, we use a cross-country regression framework: we model the historical relationship between daily gilt yield changes and those of USTs and Bunds, and treat the residual — the part of the move the global backdrop cannot explain — as the UK-specific political premium. Cumulated over the episode (8 May to 15 May), we see the residual as a clean, quantifiable measure of what the market added to gilt yields for reasons to do with idiosyncratic factors – namely, in this instance, UK politics. Second, we translate the yield premium into a supply signal. Implicitly, we assume that bond markets may in fact be pricing in the prospect of additional borrowing or, in this case, additional issuance. We think this reinforces the on-hold baseline for the BoC and argues for more two-sided risks around that modal case than market pricing implies. Benign underlying inflation (CPI-trim is back at the BoC’s target), a pickup in the unemployment rate and soft growth were the ingredients that caused a restart of the BoC’s cutting cycle late last year. And with those conditions present again, and transmission from higher oil prices to other categories limited thus far, we see further room for front-end hike premium to fade, especially in the near term. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Goods | Similar to food, slight softness ahead and pipeline pressures firming: Core goods inflation rose to 0.8%Y in April from 0.5%Y in March, above our forecast for a slight rise (0.6%Y). From the detailed print we note that clothing and footwear prices firmed more than usual in April (2.4%M vs Apr-25 at 2.1%M), which explains almost 10bp of the uptick. This led again to some volatility in the seasonally-adjusted data, following volatility in French sales and clothing and footwear (to the upside in February and downside in March) ( Exhibit 10 ). For May, we expect softness in underlying momentum and forecast that the year-on-year rate takes a small step down to 0.7%Y. Looking at pipeline pressures from our factor analysis on leading indicators, analogous to food, we note that these are firming both upstream and downstream (Exhibit 11 ). But our estimation of the pass-through suggests that it will take several months to feed into higher consumer prices, allowing for some softness near-term. W hile core CPI shows moderation, this was largely driven by a significant slowdown in housing services. Non -tradables excluding housing and fruit and vegetables increased to 2% from 1.9% . Last week’s break above 4.5% and 5.0% in n 10-year and 30-year US Treasury yields brought an uptick in rate volatility and questions about whether negative convexity dynamics may have played an amplifying role after strong performance of short gamma strategies in April, and a more sustained period of GSE mortgage purchases. On rate vol specifically, the implied volatility response has been relatively mild compared to the magnitude of the yield range shift (Exhibit 2). That noted, our estimate of gamma exposure in TY options suggests the selloff this month resulted in an abrupt shift away from “peak” gamma (which we estimate was around 4.4%); to the extent that vol sellers are less frequent/threshold hedgers (and dealers are net long vol and hedging more actively), it is possible that the sharp move resulted in a relative pick-up in short gamma hedging. On the mortgage side, although GSE-retained portfolios have grown substantially—FNMA ’s more than doubled and FHLMC’s grew by ~50% over the 12 months through March—their hedging behavior remains unclear, as the accumulation of larger duration gaps suggests increased tolerance for interest rate risk. records.text: 22 May 2026 Focus Germany Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG A look at the MoF's May 2026 Monthly Report In this update, we take a look at the May 2026 Monthly Report from the Federal Ministry of Finance (MoF), which contains the financial statistics data on federal budget developments for the first four months of the year. The analysis builds on our previous work regarding Germany's fiscal policy shift (see also here and here). It considers the latest dynamics of a) the federal government's core budget as well as b) the two major off-budgetary funds SV BW (Federal Armed Forces Fund) and SV IK (Infrastructure & Climate Protection Fund) for which the government provides monthly credit stock/flow data.1 The MoF's April 2026 budget print Monthly budgetary developments in a nutshell As Figure 1 illustrates, the total federal financing deficit (comprising the core budget, SV BW, and SV IK) rose to EUR 146 bn in April on a 12-month smoothed basis, up from approximately EUR 137 bn in March. Consequently, the total deficit, based on the trailing twelve-month sum, has expanded by around EUR 85 bn since the 2025 federal budget effectively came into force last October. Examining monthly data, the total financial deficit reached a high EUR 16 bn in April (March: c. EUR 4.5 bn). Despite this marked monthly expansion, the monthly deficit increase remained broadly in line within typical seasonal fluctuations. records.text: 54 World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 Argentina: Rating upgrade Sebastian Rondeau BofAS Fitch upgrades Argentina to B -, following IMF agreement Fitch upgraded Argentina sovereign debt to B - from CCC+, amid improving fundamentals, growing the pool of potential investors. Last month, Argentina reached a staff level agreement with the IMF that will release a $1bn loan. Argentina also announced it would get $2bn in financing from the World Bank, which could be used as a guarantee, to alleviate external debt maturities. The program demands $8bn increase in net reserves this year and zero fiscal deficit. BCRA USD purchases continue BCRA is buying USD at a good pace, accumulating about $7.5bn so far this year. It expects to buy at least $10bn this year due to a projected increase in demand for money, and good USD supply. Oil price increase benefits Argentina external accounts (as it is a net oil exporter), though it poses downward risks to our growth forecasts. The current account is approaching a balance amid commodity prices hikes and higher energy volumes. FX band limits adjust with the inflation of 2 months ago, avoiding a real appreciation of the ceiling. The government has postponed the return to global bond markets (seeking cheaper financing alternatives and privatization), despite large external debt maturities. records.text: ) that are deemed sensitive to slack. For detail, see Box 2 in "Measures of underlying inflation for the euro area ", ECB Economic Bulletin, Issue 4/2018. Persistent and Common Component of Inflation (PCCI) is one of the measures of underlying inflation monitored by the ECB. PCCI aims to capture common developments across different items in the consumption basket representing the more persistent part of inflation. PCCI is constructed using a generalised dynamic factor model, where a common factor is estimated across 12 eurozone countries and around 1000 monthly price series. The PCCI is then calculated as the weighted average of the estimated common components. Using this approach the PCCI should exclude short-term volatility due to temporary/transient factors and reflect medium- and long-run movements in inflation. See detail, Bańbura and Bobeica: PCCI – a data-rich measure of underlying inflation in the euro area , ECB Statistics Paper Series, October 2020.

records.text: JGB transaction data: April sees a recovery in JGB investment from the previous month This section in an extract from Japan Flow Update: JGB transaction data: April sees a recovery in JGB investment from the previous month, 20 May 2026. Please refer to the original report for a detailed analysis. April saw slower buying by overseas investors amid continued tensions in the Middle East, but a recovery in investment by trusts, taking JGB investment to JPY6.3trn, back to roughly the same level as in February. By maturity, overseas investors turned to net selling in superlong bonds for the first time since December 2024, but insurers switched to net buying for the first time in nine months, while the pace of net buying by trust banks also recovered, keeping net purchases above JPY1trn for a sixth straight month. In long-term bonds, overseas investors, who had been heavy net sellers the previous month, returned to net buying of JPY1.0trn, with the total recovering to around JPY2.0trn, roughly the same level as in February. In medium-term bonds, while city banks, regional banks and agricultural and forestry-related financial institutions led net purchases, foreigner buying, which had doubled in the previous month, fell sharply, but total net purchases still increased slightly from the previous month. 21 May 2026 66 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: Round and round

We continue to think the chance of cuts is much greater than hikes and think core inflation annualized closer to 2% in summer data will allow Fed officials to cut rates if/when the labor market weakens further. Our base case includes rate cuts in September, October, and December this year to a 2.75-3% policy rate. GDP rose 2.0% in Q1, due partly to a rebound in government activity following the Q4 government shutdown. Real consumption growth has been slower in recent quarters but remains resilient. We continue to expect solid growth in 2026, due partly to continued strength in AI- related business investment. The rise in energy prices, if sustained for many months, could weigh on GDP by a few tenths of a percentage point this year. Core PCE inflation has been sticky above 3%YoY while core CPI has slowed below 3%, an abnormal divergence as CPI typically runs stronger than PCE. All else equal, we estimate that reserves around 10% of bank assets would be consistent with a steady state objective of tri-party repo rates setting 1-to-2bp above IORB (rather than 1-to-2bp below, as we assume in our base case)—worth about $475bn in headroom to shrink the balance sheet in today’s terms. A policy of keeping the balance sheet stable through YE27, or shrinking by $20bn per month through 1Q27 would achieve this outcome. Shift regulatory induced demand for reserves The stigma associated with Fed liquidity facilities has undermined confidence in the tools’ ability to reliably satisfy bank demand for liquidity in periods of stress. The discount window has historically been the focal point, with banks’ reluctance to turn to it cited as detrimental to its usefulness as a backstop.2 Banks did, however, rely on intraday credit from the Fed prior to the GFC (Exhibit 13), with daylight overdrafts—which arise when banks overdraw their Fed accounts during the day in order to make payments but return to a non-negative position by end of day—growing over time with the banking system. records.text: M Idea 6 The effective tariff rate and tariff receipts The tariff rate on US imports has fallen to 8.3% in 1Q26 data On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court struck down the President's authority to impose tariffs under IEEPA. Section 122 tariffs will replace IEEPA tariffs in the short term, though uncertainty rises after the 150-day period when Congress would need to extend those tariffs. Replacing IEEPA with Section 122 tariffs of 15% and considering composition effects of US imports, we estimate baseline tariffs near 11%. Our estimate of "core" tariffs (ex fuels, gold and AI-related imports) remains closer to 13-14%. In our view, near-term tariffs are likely capped below 'Liberation Day' levels—at least until Section 232 and 301 investigations are complete. In the March 2026 data, the effective tariff rate is estimated at ~7%, and the 1Q26 tariff rate averages to 8.3%. records.text: European High Yield Dissecting the UK Premium UK political uncertainty has driven £HY underperformance, pushing the £-€ yield differential to 2.5%, above the peak in 2023. However, much of the premium is composition-driven (lower-quality bias), with adjusted valuations closer to fair value and limited pricing of UK-specific growth shocks. • UK-driven volatility has pushed £HY to wide headline levels, with underperformance vs €• driving the yield differential to 2.5%, breaking above the previous peak reached in late-2023. • However, much of the apparent cheapness is composition-driven, with £HY’s lower-• quality skew inflating spreads and yields relative to €HY. Rebasing the £HY index on €HY ratings composition reduces the yield pick-up to 50bp. • Looking at the 'UK premium' over European and US corporates in the broader PE HY index• also shows a similar trend with the headline pick-up (of 180bp and 230bp respectively) compressing to just c.115bp once lower-rated credits are excluded. • The cyclical to non-cyclical spread gap has also edged lower year-to-date with only• minimal repricing on the back of recent developments, and at just over 100bp, remains well below levels seen in previous growth stress periods (in late-2022 and 2020). With oil prices staying high, concerns over rising inflation intensified this week and US yields also rose sharply, but USDJPY remained largely unchanged at around 159, partly because it again approached levels that raise concern over FX intervention. FM Katayama also continued her verbal intervention this week, saying that the authorities would “take resolute action when action is needed” on FX moves. In this context, USDJPY looks likely to remain capped by intervention concerns for the time being. If Middle East tensions ease, JPY selling may temporarily subside, but if developments lead to accelerated JPY selling, caution will be needed over possible FX intervention at the start of the week when overseas markets are on holiday. The cocktail of weaker growth and higher inflation is distasteful for central banks—With the economy’s momentum looking to have remained intact, the markets are increasingly emphasizing the risk of higher inflation and, accordingly, are pricing in less supportive policy paths. The markets now see almost a full hike from the Fed by year-end, three hikes from the ECB, and two or three hikes from the Bank of England. In tandem, long-term interest rates are surging upward as well. Can growth remain solid if oil prices are stubbornly above $100/barrel?—The jury is still out on this question. The global economy has shown surprising resilience since the onset of the conflict and, more broadly, has shaken off a variety of shocks in recent years. In addition, global inventories are providing a substantial buffer, and oil prices as high as $110/barrel are not unprecedented. From 2011 through the first half of 2014, oil prices ran at similarly high levels and global growth was solid. Despite the signs of resilience, we remain cautious—These are still early days in terms of global adjustment to the oil shock. records.text: Japan Economics 22 May 2026 Citi Research 2 April nationwide CPI: Special factors weigh on inflation The nationwide core CPI (excluding only fresh food) increased 1.4% YoY in April, down by 0.4ppt from a 1.8% YoY advance in March. The result was much weaker than the market projection (+1.7%) and marked the lowest level since March 2022. Meanwhile, CPI excluding fresh food and energy, i.e., core-core CPI, rose 1.9% YoY in April, down by 0.5ppt from a 2.4% YoY increase in March and undershooting the market projection for a 2.2% YoY advance. Core-core inflation fell below 2% for the first time since July 2024. Core CPI and overall CPI came in below 2% for a third consecutive month for the former and a fourth consecutive month for the latter. We note, however, that the large part of the decline was attributable to special policy factors rather than indicating weaker underlying inflation pressure directly (see our discussion below). The main factor driving core CPI down was slower food inflation (-0.26ppt contribution), which in turn stemmed mainly from the free public elementary school lunch program started in April (-0.12ppt contribution). School lunch prices (at elementary school) plunged by 98.0% YoY in April. In addition, the introduction of free private high school tuition in April sent high school tuition (private) down by 68.8% YoY, pushing down overall CPI by 0.18ppt. records.text: Not Too Worried About the April Data Miss China’s April activity data surprised significantly to the downside, with industrial production (IP), retail sales, and fixed asset investment (FAI) all missing market expectations by a large margin. Exhibit 1 shows that the downside surprise was the largest since May 2023, when China’s post-Covid reopening activity disappointed. Is Chinese growth momentum on the ground really decelerating sharply? We think not. In this note, we explain that, although the Middle East conflict and higher energy prices have indeed taken a toll on certain industries, the broad macroeconomic picture in China has not changed much. Strong exports and weak domestic demand remain the key features of the Chinese economy at present. Going forward, two key things to watch are (1) whether export strength, especially to low-income oil-importing EM destinations, is sustained in the face of the global energy-supply shock, and (2) whether the property market continues to show signs of stabilization in top-tier cities. IP Data Shows Impact of the Iran War IP growth slowed notably from 5.7% yoy in March to 4.1% yoy in April, nearly 2pp lower than the Bloomberg consensus expectation of 6.0% yoy. Policy implications: The need for an early rate hike remains unchanged The weaker-than-expected April CPI data will likely reduce the probability of an additional rate hike by the BoJ at its June meeting. The reasons cited by Governor Ueda and board members for holding off on a rate hike at the April meeting included "lower certainty in the outlook," a judgment that "the situation does not require a hasty rate hike," and the need to "assess the pass-through of rising crude oil prices to households." The latest CPI results could be interpreted as reinforcing the rationale for this cautious stance. We maintain our view that the BoJ should have proceeded with an additional rate hike in April, given the build-up of underlying inflationary pressures, and that an early normalization of monetary policy is desirable. However, taking the decision to pause in April as a given, we believe it will be difficult to gather sufficient justification for a rate hike in June based on this data alone. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 3 Household survey: weakness worth watching However, the Household survey was weak in April. Household employment declined by 226k, marking the fourth consecutive drop and creating a divergence from the Establishment survey’s NFP (Nonfarm Payroll) print. This divergence is not uncommon, and we typically place more weight on the Establishment survey signal, given the survey's lower standard error (~120k vs ~500k). But the Household survey signal is still worth monitoring (Exhibit 2). Also, broader slack measures showed some weakness: U6 rose to 8.2% (highest since 2021), part-time workers for economic reasons saw an increase and unemployment duration rose as well. Labor force participation edged down to 61.8%, driven by the 55+ cohort, while prime-age participation held steady, an important offset. Overall, we see the labor market as solid, but not necessarily heating up. Wages: steady, not inflationary When judging whether the labor market is becoming hot and potentially inflationary, wage dynamics are key. One metric we track closely is the wage premium for job switchers. Measures of this premium, including from our Bank of America Institute, do not suggest the labor market has tightened to start the year. Atlanta Fed data show some modest firming after the premium effectively disappeared between mid-2024 and mid-2025. To help fill this void, we construct indicative total return trackers (TRTs) for US CPI swaps since 2014, covering spot tenors from 1-30y, as well as a few select major forwards (1y1y, 2yfwd3y, 5y5y, 10y10y, 20yfwd10y, 10yfwd20y). For more details on the methodology, see the first Appendix in the full report. Total return tracker performance At a high level, since the beginning of 2014, we find that inflation swap performance has gone through three regimes ( Figure 3). First was pre-COVID, which was characterized by somewhat choppy performance — a notable sell-off in 2014 alongside the shale revolution, a meaningful rally in 2016 as President Trump was elected the first time, and a grind lower to close out the decade. By contrast, after troughing in March 2020, inflation swaps went into a significant bull run through April 2022 (not coincidentally, the FOMC finally started hiking rates in March 2022). Much of the decrease was driven by a 10.2% decline in auto fuel sales after a sharp rise in March. But sales volumes excluding auto fuel also fell, by 0.4%mom, with retailers citing poor weather but also weak demand and greater consumer price sensitivity. Taken together with yesterday’s flash PMI figures for May, the latest data are consistent with the view that growth is likely to slow notably after a strong Q1 as higher energy prices weigh on output. If the conflict is not resolved soon, there could be further air pockets and headwinds ahead. One particular concern is that every day that passes with the Strait remaining closed means a further drawing down of accumulated global inventories. While these stocks strike us as likely to be sufficient for still some time, it’s admittedly unclear how low these inventory levels can safely go. The remainder of our note is composed of two sections. The first focuses on the recent performance of global inflation and the implications for central bank policy. In this context, we also consider the sharp recent rise in longer-term global interest rates. The final section discusses some risk scenarios for the global economy, including the upside possibility that global resilience continues. That said, we think that the shock will be short-lived, with inflation falling back to 2.7% next year. At the country level, many of the mark-ups are significant (Figure 10). records.text: April Trade: Crude Oil Import Unit Price Surges while Import Volume Plunges. Stable LNG Import Price Trade data for April show that export value posted double-digit growth for the second consecutive month, at +14.8% yoy. Import value maintained a similar pace of increase to March (+10.9%), at +9.7% yoy. As a result, the trade balance swung to a surplus of +¥301.9 bn, from a small deficit of -¥149.5 bn in April of last year. Export volume maintained a similar pace of increase in April as the January-March average of +3.6%, at +3.4% yoy. However, on a seasonally adjusted mom basis (our calculation), volume declined by -2.9% mom in April (Jan-Mar quarter: +3.9% qoq). While export volume to the US and Europe increased sharply yoy, exports to Asia slowed. Regarding crude oil imports, a point of concern since the worsening of the situation in the Middle East, the unit price calculated from import value and volume had not yet risen significantly as of March. However, prices rose sharply in April to ¥16,121/bl (March: ¥10,763/bl), or US$101.4/bl (March: US$68.7/bl) in US dollar terms. This represents a sharp rise of +57% and +54%, respectively, compared to February (pre-conflict). On a yoy basis, prices turned to an increase of +38% and +28% (they were down -10% yoy in March). Crude oil import volume dropped by -63.7% yoy. While CPI swaps don't just reflect inflation expectations, and likely capture an elevated inflation risk premium, the nominal or real rate markets are likely to also reflect that as additional risk premium. Hence, we believe that the asymmetry in the front-end does not arise so much from the real policy rate being too high but rather from the inflation rate being too high. Our inflation strategists have argued here that 1yf inflation is embedding too much risk premium for pass- through into core inflation from recent events, given the subdued outlook for shelter inflation and the general lack of wage pressures. A quick resolution of the Iran war should likely lead to less pass-through than is expected and lower inflation swap rates. A delayed resolution need not push 1yf inflation that much higher. We would look to Chair-designate Warsh's reaction function on how tolerant he will be with inflation in a 2-handle to assess if the implied real policy rate is high or low. With current yield and duration profiles, we estimate that HY yields can rise by roughly 15bp per month while still delivering positive total returns. A slow grind higher in yields, therefore, need not meaningfully undermine demand. Putting this together, higher rates do not in themselves derail strong credit markets, provided the pace is measured. The main domestic private demand items of private consumption and capex maintained their upward trend, and the positive contribution from external demand expanded. The only negative contributions were from a slight decrease in inventories (-0.2 pp) and an increase in imports (which is a deduction item for GDP and thus was a negative contributor). No items showed exceptional movements from special factors, and we see that Q1 growth was well-balanced between domestic and external demand. Private Consumption Continues to See Moderate Increase in Services Consumption: Private consumption accelerated to +1.1% qoq annualized from +0.2% in Q4, maintaining positive growth for the fifth consecutive quarter. A breakdown shows that while durable goods turned negative at -5.5% qoq annualized, semi-durable goods (+3.6%), non-durable goods (+1.7%), and services consumption (+0.8%) increased. This semi-annual exercise lays out our core views for the next 12 months and allows us to take stock of how much things have changed. One shift has been in energy. Back in November, the world looked awash with oil. Now it looks uncomfortably short. Our base case assumes that the Strait of Hormuz opens in June, with a longer disruption a key risk to our views. We are watching inventory levels closely. Yet even more notable has been the strength of activity despite geopolitics. Six months ago, we expected the US economy to grow +1.8% in 2026 and +2.0% in 2027. Those figures are currently +2.3% and +2.6%. We estimated S&P 500 earnings growth would be (an above-consensus) +17% for 2026. We now see +23%. Several factors explain this resilience. One is inelasticity: demand that is proving surprisingly resistant to higher prices, higher financing costs, and higher geopolitical risk. Strong balance sheets, from technology companies and households, are allowing it to continue. It starts with the AI infrastructure buildout, this year’s most important macro and micro story. records.text: US Rates Weekly 22 May 2026 Citi Research 11 Vol: Shifting gamma shorts from 1y tails to 2y Short-expiry vols on 1y tails have cheapened meaningful, while 2y tails have stayed resilient. We prefer to express our short upper-left bias on 3m2y going forward. We have rolled our receiver calendar spread from 1y tails to 2y tails for a profit and entered into a costless 3m2y 1x2 payer spread to fade the tail risk of multiple consecutive rate hikes. Gamma on 2y tails can cheapen and converge toward 1y tails Selling short-expiry vol on front-end rates on any near-term bounce while the Fed remains divided has been one of our core views, and the vol market has repriced accordingly. Looking at the vol term structures across the tails, one can see a clear distinction between the 1y tails and all the others. The shorter expiries on the 1y tails have already cheapened and are trading well below the longer expiries, resulting in an upward sloping vol term structure that peaks at the 1y expiry (Figure 20). In contrast, the vol term structures for the other tails are still relatively flat. This difference is especially pronounced around the 3m and 6m expiries, where the 3m1y/6m1y vol ratio has been steadily declining since early April to 0.86 currently (the vol slope has been steepening), while the 3m2y/6m2y vol ratio is trading just below 1 (Figure 21). records.text: The RBA communication at its latest meeting in May suggests that it believes its three consecutive rate hikes thus far have provided room to pause and assess the situation. As a result, we think the risk-reward favors paying the RBA's August meeting instead, which will follow the release of Q2 inflation data and an updated Statement of Monetary Policy (SoMP). Looking ahead, we expect the Australian economy to remain resilient, driven by its status as a net energy exporter and supported by government and fiscal measures, which will be bolstered by increased tax revenues. While consumer sentiment may remain weak and discretionary spending subdued if the Middle East conflict persists, the RBA has indicated that it is comfortable with lower growth, as it believes the economy's output gap remains positive and that a period of slow growth is necessary to bring demand and supply back into balance. In the event of a de-escalation in the Middle East, we anticipate that Australia's energy exports will continue to be supported, while the rebound in risk sentiment may keep the RBA focused on upside risks to inflation, given its assessment that the economy is already operating above capacity. Trade: Pay June/Aug RBA at 10.75bp in 20k/01. Target: 25bp. Stop: 0bp. What makes AI different is that it can have an impact across a broader part (sectors) of the economy. Small improvements on this front can easily magnify the impact on aggregate productivity 10 times over the next decade (see below for some examples). But crucially, AI can also increase the productivity of innovation, i.e. it has the potential to affect cognitive work and the generation of ideas. In other words, it can make innovation more productive. This is what, in the long term, can make AI go beyond a one-off level effect on productivity to impacting productivity growth. It can potentially lead to an increase in the growth rate of productivity, taking the economy to a faster (permanent) trajectory, in an optimistic scenario. It takes time though, as we saw with IT, for the new ideas that are possible to new technologies to arrive. In the meantime, countries that are better positioned to convert AI into durable productivity gains such as the US and China are more likely to have larger one-off effects in productivity and be closer to the more optimistic scenario. The average country in Europe, instead, is unlikely to benefit as much absent substantial reforms. The impact would likely be even smaller in countries in EEMEA and in LatAm. records.text: The selection of Kevin Warsh as the next Chair of the Federal Reserve has n brought renewed attention to the Fed’s balance sheet policy. Fed officials have voiced support for the ample reserves framework in recent months, but acknowledged that evidence of a reduction in reserve demand would warrant an adjustment in the supply of reserves. The year-to-date moderation in US Dollar funding volatility suggests the Fed has n room to allow reserves to gradually decline as a share of bank assets while anchoring funding costs modestly below interest on reserve balances. We expect monthly balance sheet growth to average $5bn until early 2027 before returning to a trend-like pace of $25bn per month to keep reserves stable around 11% of bank assets. A stable balance sheet would see reserves drop to the 2019 lows as a share of bank assets by the end of the decade. We expect Fed ownership of Treasuries as a share of the market to rise gradually n but remain below the pre-GFC average, even as the Fed buys USTs to grow the balance sheet and replace MBS runoff. Keeping the balance sheet stable and just reinvesting MBS runoff into USTs would see the Fed’s share of the market decline. records.text: US Rates Weekly 22 May 2026 Citi Research 15 USTs: Private demand picks up Data on foreign holdings of USTs (TIC) for the month of March showed that demand for long-term USTs picked up in March after a slight decrease in February. Overall, foreign holdings of long-term USTs increased by $56.1bn on a value- adjusted basis (Figure 28). The increase was mainly driven by foreign private investors, whose long-term UST holdings increased by about $80.5bn (z-score of 1.15). On the other hand, foreign official long-term UST holdings decreased by about $24bn (z-score of -0.74). Overall, in the first three months of the year, foreign investors purchased $105.1bn of long-term USTs which was slightly less than what we saw in the first quarter of 2025 ($162.1bn). After buying $91.6bn of T-bills in February, foreign investors reduced their T-bill holdings by $16.8bn in March (z-score of -0.76). Both foreign official and foreign private investors have reduced their T-bill holdings by $12.1bn and $4.7bn respectively. We don’t think most of the declines are outright sales but rather maturities from some of the T-bills purchased in February. On a market value basis, the Treasury reported a net decrease of $121bn in foreign UST holdings in March. Previously published in CTD switch risk in higher rate environment, May 21, 2025. • Higher yields increase CTD switch risk and reduce predictability in futures DV01 and• basis convergence. The conversion factor (CF) system anchors pricing at 6%, and as market yields move towards this level, dispersion across deliverable bonds compresses and the value of the delivery switch option increases. • Low dispersion across the deliverable basket can lead to frequent CTD shifts. Small• changes in relative value, repo, the curve shape, or delivery timing can trigger CTD switches, making it difficult to identify the CTD ex-ante and can complicate hedging and trading with the basket. Liquidity premia could build around neighboring securities in the delivery basket as the likelihood of any of them being CTD increases. • Basis dynamics become more sensitive to switch risk. records.text: World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 33 Taiwan: Energy lifts inflation Xiaoqing Pi Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Taiwan CPI inflation picked up on energy price Taiwan's CPI inflation picked up to 1.74% yoy in Apr . The rise in headline CPI was driven primarily by energy (around 10.8% yoy), although the effective pass through remained moderated by the government's fuel price smoothing mechanism. Goods and services inflation rose to 1.1% and 2.3% yoy, respectively (fr om 0.2% and 2.2% in Mar), suggesting a modest broadening of price pressures . Looking ahead, we expect inflation to rise toward around 2% in May, assuming elevated global oil prices as in our base case and relatively stable domestic fuel pricing. Strong consumption momentum, together with the yoy TWD depreciation , is likely to add to near term inflationary pressure -indeed, import prices in TWD terms were already up 9.2% yoy in April. That said, any renewed appreciation of the TWD - would help mitigate imported inflation and partially cushion the impact of higher ener gy prices Export growth softened in April, but momentum stays steady Apr exports slowed to 39.0% yoy ( -15.7% mom) after Mar's spike . We see it as normalization plus a high Apr 2025 base. Momentum stays tech-led, with info & comm (62.3% yoy) and electronic components (+38.9% yoy), consistent with resilient AI demand. Looking ahead, we think export growth should stay supported as long as AI - related demand remains resilient, with ongoing capacity expansion

Drawing on the academic literature linking bond supply to yield levels, we invert that relationship, assessing what a given basis point premium implies for a specific amount of additional annual net gilt issuance. What does our model suggest about potential supply? The Model: We start with a simple model to estimate political risk premia. Our regression is estimated on daily yield changes rather than levels, which matters for two reasons. First, yield levels are non-stationary — they drift over cycles in ways that can generate spurious correlations — whereas daily changes are stationary and reflect genuine market reactions to news. Second, working in daily changes allows us to isolate the market's reaction on each specific day, which is important in an episode like this one where the political narrative was evolving rapidly: the local election results on 7 May, the resignation calls from over 70 Labour MPs the following week, and the clearing of Burnham to contest the Makerfield by-election – each leaving a distinct footprint in the daily residuals. Standard errors are estimated using the Newey-West procedure, which corrects for the autocorrelation and volatility clustering inherent in daily financial data and ensures that any premium we identify is statistically robust rather than an artefact of market noise. 4 US Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 Special factors When thinking about the labor market outlook for 2026 and 2027, it is important to take into account a few factors: the upcoming World Cup, summer weakness in jobs, the supply shock from tighter immigration policies and its impact on breakven job growth, and risks of QCEW-driven payroll revisions. i) World Cup effect: temporary, modest boost The 2026 FIFA World Cup (June-July) is likely to provide a temporary lift to payrolls, particularly in leisure & hospitality, trade & transportation, construction and professional & business services. Some headline estimates suggest ~185k jobs could be added. However, several factors will likely limit the measured immediate impact on payrolls: i) a significant portion of demand will likely be met via overtime (which does not increase payrolls), rather than temporary hiring, ii) independent contractor usage (e.g., security, logistics) is not captured in the Establishment survey, and iii) regular visitors are expected to avoid host cities (tourism substitution), and this would offset some of the boost from the World Cup. Looking at Copa America 2024, roughly one-quarter the scale of the World Cup in terms of attendance, we saw no discernible impact on national payrolls. Hence, we pencil in only a modest temporary bump, which is expected to play out as follows: i) June: about a 40k bump in payrolls, primarily via temporary leisure & hospitality hiring, ii) July: no impact from the World Cup

records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 21 May 2026 3 AI is about to lift macro productivity So far, AI’s macro‑level productivity impact remains limited. While evidence shows large task‑level (micro) productivity gains, AI has barely moved aggregate productivity, echoing the early phases of past breakthroughs such as electricity and ICT. But AI is different: its scale, general‑purpose nature, and boost to innovation mean long‑run gains could far exceed what we are currently seeing. Indeed, we expect fast adopters like the US and China to be the first to show a clear rise in macro productivity —specifically higher total factor productivity. That would raise the marginal product of capital, lift investment, and push up r*. But the overall global path for r* remains uncertain: higher inequality, a falling labor share of income, and aging populations may increase desired household savings, offsetting, or even reversing, part of the upward push from investment. Meanwhile, we think that slower adopters (Europe/EM) risk persistent productivity (and r*) divergence. AI and productivity: Big micro, small macro—for now There is clear evidence that AI is sizably increasing productivity at the micro level. But the more we move away from the micro to the aggregate (macro), the smaller the impact becomes. These findings suggest that short-term aggregate effects are dampened by heterogeneity across firms and sectors (Exhibit 1). In the near-term, the attention will be on whether Andy Burnham can win the Makerfield by-election (likely 18 June, the same day as the BoE meeting). Gilts are already under pressure from the possibility, but if he secures a seat back in Westminster another leg of cheapening is likely. records.text: Danny Suwanapruti +65-6889-1987 | danny.suwanapruti@gs.com Goldman Sachs (Singapore) Pte Global Markets Daily: Asia Finding it Harder to Look Through the Energy Shock 21 May 2026 | 5:49PM SGT Since the start of the Middle East conflict, the overall impact on growth in Asia n has been less than feared, partly due to inventory drawdowns, less demand destruction than expected, and impressive AI-related export growth. Meanwhile, inflation has risen steadily across the region and, in some cases, has surprised significantly to the upside. For most of the economies in the region, the primary policy response to the n energy shock was fiscal. However, with no clear path for a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, oil prices still elevated (Brent at US$100–110/bbl), inflation creeping higher, and Asian currencies coming under significant pressure, policymakers are finding it increasingly difficult to simply “look through” the shock. The Philippines central bank hiked by 25bp in April, and Bank Indonesia hiked by 50bp in May. Our economists think the CBC, BoK, and RBI will join the tightening cycle, n although the five hikes currently priced into the KRW and INR curves appear too aggressive. Korea is facing a K-shaped recovery, heavily skewed toward Tech, and we therefore do not expect an aggressive BoK hiking cycle. records.text: mployment • Given the recent upside surprises in the labor data, we are upgrading our labor market forecasts modestly. Our payroll averages for 2026 and 2027 are now 66k (previous: 45k) and 69k (previous: 43k). Our new payroll trajectory accounts for the impact of the World Cup and summer weakness in hiring. We still think that the supply shock from tighter immigration policies implemented since last year is an important narrative driver in the labor market and hence breakeven job growth continues to be at about 20k. We expect the u-rate to stay around 4.3% in ’26 and 4.2% in ’27. However, our broader message is unchanged. This is a stable labor market that has bottomed out, not one that is overheating. Fed: on hold in 2026 and pushing cuts out to 2H27 • The Fed held rates steady at 3.5-3.75% at its Apr meeting and maintained its easing bias in the statement, as we were expecting. But there were three dissents in favor of removing this bias. Powell’s presser was a bit hawkish. We no longer expect the Fed to cut rates this year. We have pushed the two cuts in our forecast out from Sep-Oct '26 to Jul-Sep '27. The terminal rate stays at 3.0-3.25%. records.text: Euro Area: Rates Strategy Caught in crosscurrents EUR rates continue to be pushed around by energy market developments and SOFR spillovers. We take stock of the outlook for ECB pricing, outline our constructive view on DSLs and update our EUR swap positioning indicators. European rates have been subjected to both bearish and bullish cross-market spillovers in recent days, resulting in continued choppy price action. On the bearish side, sticky US core inflation and US labour market resilience had been driving a reappraisal of Fed pricing, with rate cut pricing replaced by premia for a potential Fed hike. More recently, however, markets have swung from fear to hope once again with respect to the US-Iran conflict, on reports that the two parties may be close to a peace deal. This brought fresh downward pressures on oil prices on Wednesday, resulting in pricing out of rate hikes across developed markets. On the data front, Thursday's euro area PMIs painted a bleak picture of the growth outlook, for both services and manufacturing (in France especially), with the composite print falling to 47.5 versus consensus of 48.8. On the inflation side of the equation, the input price index continued to climb sharply to 70.5 (a level not seen since 2022); increases to the output price index were more modest, with this component edging higher to 56.9. Given trend growth in non-reserve Fed liabilities and the size of the banking system, a stable Fed balance sheet size would result in a steady decline in reserves of about $150bn per year in absolute terms and 1.2 percentage points per year as a share of bank assets. We think an extended period of balance sheet stability is plausible, leaving clear downside risks to our reserve baseline. But we think the bar to a meaningful decline in the size of the balance sheet is high given the organic erosion of relative reserve supply over time, uncertainty around the timing and ultimate impact of potential regulatory adjustments, and the challenges with observing system-wide reserve needs in real-time. The potential costs that could arise from overshooting—elevated funding volatility and challenges to Treasury market function—raise the risk that going too far requires a sharp rebuild in the size of the balance sheet—as was seen in both 2019 and 2025. Beyond the considerations related to reserve demand, our economists have highlighted likely challenges to Warsh’s argument that shrinking the Fed’s balance sheet would create room to lower the funds rate. A higher free float—the stock of Treasuries outstanding held by non-Fed buyers—would typically bias longer-term yields higher and push swap spreads tighter. The two-thirds majority allows Tisza to structurally reform Hungary after 16 years under Fidesz, from macro to the judiciary, to rule of law. Together with Tisza’s euro ambition, there is likely more political capital for the new government to take some difficult economic decisions to reduce the fiscal burden, supporting policies to rein in inflation. EU funds will be unblocked, with potential inflows of c.5% of GDP this year, including EUR6.5bn grants from the Recovery and Resilience Facility. In the longer term, the EUR roadmap is a positive structural theme for Hungary. A better relationship with the EU and more business-friendly environment will also help promote investments and attract foreign direct investments. We expect growth to recover to 2 -3% in the coming years. In view of structurally lower risk premia, the NBH likely has room to cut rates sooner – we bring forward our rate-cut expectations to June but still forecast the policy rate to reach 4.5% in 2027. records.text: important driver, low distressed exposure should remain supportive for continued convert performance, as contained credit stress limits downside pressure from weaker issuers. Convertible defaults have remained low, though recoveries bear monitoring: Thus far in 2026, the overall U.S. convertible default rate, across bonds, preferreds, and mandatory structures, stands at 0.23%, below the 1.95% default rate in 2025 and the long-term average since 2003 of 1.26%. This suggests default activity remains contained despite a more volatile macro backdrop. Recoveries on recent defaults have remained below the long-term average of 30.4%, underscoring the importance of issuer selection, liquidity analysis, and capital-structure seniority in weaker credits. Convertible bond default rates are again lower than HY: On a bonds-only basis, the YTD U.S. convertible bond default rate of 0.3% is below the HY par-weighted default rate of 1.9%. This marks a notable improvement from 2025, when the convertible bond default rate reached 2.2%, above the HY default rate of 1.5%. The latest data are more consistent with the longer-term pattern of lower convertible bond defaults versus HY, supporting the case that convert credit risk remains contained despite a more volatile macro backdrop. Despite low distress and limited defaults, credit discipline remains important: The sharp decline in default risk and still-low distressed exposure are constructive, and a sustained primary calendar remains supportive

records.text: UK: Rates Strategy High cortisol market The gilt market remains in thrall to political headlines and economic uncertainty. But from a technical perspective, the curve looks very steep given favourable supply dynamics over the summer and front-end valuations. It was another week of volatility in sterling rates with the market simultaneously coming under pressure from economic and political headlines. Figure 1 shows the benchmark gilt yield curve on 30 April after the publication of the latest MPR, the closing level on 20 May and the min-max range of benchmark yields since the local elections (7 May). The yield curve overall is fairly near levels at the time of the April MPR. But the range over the past two weeks has been between 20-28bp in post 5yr maturities. This week's heavyweight data slate brought the MPC's profile of tightening over 2026 into focus. Both the labour market and inflation data were unambiguously soft, with the unemployment rate rising and vacancies falling to a five-year low. Inflation surprised to the downside with both headline and core measures of the closely-watched services inflation series softer than expected. Traditionally volatile items such as airfares and holidays were all weaker and importantly there were no signs of pass-though from energy prices to the wider inflation basket. records.text: A Constructive Outlook for Spanish Debt Investors are constructive on Spanish bonds as weakening momentum due to the energy crisis seems to have been unaffected by country-specific risks. In line with previous work, we use a simple structural vector autoregression (SVAR) model with “sign restrictions” to disentangle the underlying macro drivers of sovereign debt pricing. To do so, we define the drivers as follows: 1. Euro Area Shock: when both the Spanish and German sovereign yield curve flatten (10y-2y Bonos and 10y-2y Bund) and the Spanish sovereign spread (10y Bonos-Bund) widens. 2. Domestic Shock: when only the Spanish sovereign yield curve flattens and the Spanish sovereign spread widens at the same time. 3. Long-End Rates Sell-off: when both the Spanish and German sovereign yield curves steepen and the Spanish sovereign spread widens. In this simple way, it is possible to assess whether the market pricing of Spanish sovereign spreads is more likely to be due to external macro factors – e.g., a deteriorated growth outlook or inflation surging in the region, with rates selling off – or to risk factors specific to the Spanish landscape that push up the yield curve and widen the sovereign spread at the same time. We find that domestic risk (a flatter Spanish curve and wider spread) has remained contained throughout the energy shock so far, while spread widening has been combined with flatter yield curves across Europe. However, activity, construction, and employment statistics continue to struggle in a stop-go pattern, while declining government confidence raises questions about the reform program’s social sustainability. We believe the program is driven by genuine social demand rather than government imposition alone, suggesting continuity is likely despite some unforced political errors that have eroded public support. records.text: Spain – Structural Resilience Beyond the Energy Shock Spain’s macro outperformance remains visible both in economic activity and in sovereign debt pricing. Economic activity has continued to run ahead of the Euro area and the US since the middle of last year, while sovereign spreads have remained comparatively tight, indicating investors’ confidence in the outlook for Spain. That said, the Spanish economy is set to slow down because of the energy shock, although it is still outperforming the Euro area (Exhibit 1). Current macroeconomic performance compares favourably from an historical standpoint. Spain entered this energy crisis from a relatively robust macro position. Even accounting for the upcoming slowdown, we forecast real GDP growth in 2026 at or above the long-run average, while the primary fiscal balance compares favourably with historical precedents and is the third-highest in the last 19 years (Exhibit 2). records.text: deliver (CTD) switches. We previously highlighted the dynamic in long-end Treasury futures when bond yields first crossed above 5% in the second half of 2023 (see here). This poses challenges for asset managers using futures overlays for duration hedging. It also has implications for leveraged participants and primary dealers who are on the other side of asset manager long positions, as they are effectively long the futures cash basis ( Figure 1). CTD switches introduce uncertainty in basis behavior, complicate hedging behavior, and disrupt carry/convergence mechanics. Another important dynamic is long-end yields rising towards 6%, the level embedded in the conversion factor calculation that the CME uses. There is greater CTD switch risk, and the dispersion in relative value across the deliverable basket compresses. In contrast to the post- GFC regime, in which CTDs can be identified ex-ante, multiple securities are likely to cluster as close CTDs, which increases the frequency and unpredictability of switches. Hedgers may need to adjust hedge ratios when using futures as a derivatives overlay. Frequent CTD switches could also affect the economics and convergence mechanics of futures basis trades. At yields above 6%, Treasury bonds with coupons higher than 6% could enter the deliverable basket with a conversion factor greater than 1, which has not occurred in this generation, given the broad-based decline in long-end yields over the past three decades ( Figure 2). Meanwhile, the DRC is one of the largest sulphur buyers globally and much of that material is converted into sulphuric acid on site. Given these constraints, we estimate that around 1Mt of copper supply is at risk in the DRC, equivalent to 3% of global supply. Tightness in sulphur is also feeding through into the downstream sulphuric acid market. Indeed, China said it would suspend sulphuric acid sales abroad from May , an issue because the count ry is one of the largest exporters. The implications are numerous. While Glencore notes that current sulphuric acid dislocations do not impact operations in the DRC because feedstock is available from alternative suppliers, albeit at a higher price, other operators in the country are more exposed. Also, Chile is among the largest sulphuric acid importers , with China, Peru and Japan accounting for around three-quarters of those purchases. While producers have so far been able to diversify sulfuric acid purchases, there are still concerns that Chilean production could ultimately come under pressure. Already now, production costs at those operations which run open pit mines and need to use sulfuric have risen by 30%, factoring in also higher diesel prices . Pre-Iran war, we expected the fiscal deficit to remain elevated at 5.3% of GDP in 2026, only modestly declining to 4.6% of GDP in 2027. Our 2026 assumptions were consistent with crude oil production of 10.2mn bpd, oil prices of US$60/bbl, and robust non-oil revenues.
