records.text: ion above highlights that the long-term impact of AI on aggregate productivity will depend on how well AI diffuses across companies (beyond frontier ones), how those companies reorganize themselves, whether workers adapt, the existence of legal or regulatory constraints and AI’s ability to increase the productivity of idea generation. All these variables can amplify the one-off effect on productivity and make it more likely that we end up with a permanent shift in the growth rate of productivity (the optimistic scenario), rather than just a one-level effect. The US and China are way ahead of the average European country on diffusion, structural readiness and (although less so) adaptability in terms of AI potential development, and a ranking on a forthcoming Winners and Losers report makes this clear. records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 22 May) Real GDP grew +2.1% q/q saar in Q1 (Q4: +0.8%), remaining in positive territory for a second consecutive quarter and slightly exceeding Bloomberg consensus and our forecast (both +1.7%). Consumption accelerated, while exports also picked up sharply, making the largest contribution, against the backdrop of firm goods exports to Asia and a recovery in exports to the US. That said, the strong Q1 result had yet to fully reflect the impact of Middle East tensions, which intensified from late February onward. Looking ahead, higher energy prices stemming from these developments will weigh on both consumption and capex. If supply constraints in products such as naphtha materialize, the impact could expand in a non-linear manner. If tensions in the Middle East begin to ease, we would expect firms to resume active investment aimed at rebuilding supply chains to cope with labor shortages, while consumption also recovers, supported by large wage hikes. From the H2 FY26 onward, the fiscal policy of the Takaichi administration, which is aiming for a high-pressure economy, is also expected to provide some support for growth. On the price front, BoJ core inflation slowed more than expected in April, partly reflecting institutional factors, but looking ahead we expect the impact of higher oil prices and JPY weakness to gradually emerge as upside pressure. records.text: 4 World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 USD: underpriced upside risks Alex Cohen BofAS Themes: the limits of policy divergence We maintain a near-term bullish dollar bias, as t he DXY remains within its historically narrow 12-month range. Since the start of the Iran war , the USD has done a full round trip: first appreciating along with the initial spike higher in oil, then subsequently depreciating following the April ceasefire announcement. As the market awaits more clarity on this front, the broader consolidation in front -month oil futures amid hope for some resolution has kept FX volatility and the USD mostly suppressed. Upside risks appear underpriced. Beyond the war, the USD has received only modest support thus far from the string of upside US data, including labor, retail sales and inflation . From a monetary policy standpoint, this has resulted in only a modest pricing of Fed hikes throughout the curve, as the market remains reluctant to materially price the upper end of the fed funds distribution. In comparison, a much more significant number of hikes have been priced into several other G10 central bank curves . Given relative economic outlooks, centra l bank pricing seems more likely to converge than diverge from here. Forecasts: more USD upside into Q2, before deprecation resumes We keep our G10 FX forecasts unchanged. We continue to further USD upside through H2, before modestly depreciating by year ’s end. We see headline and core PCE inflation at 3.2% and 2.8% this year, and 2.0% and 2.3% next year (each 4Q/4Q). If our baseline outlook for benign de-escalation is correct, the Fed is on hold through year-end, then easing 25bp in March and June of 2027. Markets disagree and appear aligned with a weighted average of our "permanent oil premium" and "aggregate demand" alternative scenarios, where persistently high energy prices and AI-related demand effects keep inflation firm (see the alternative scenarios from our Mid-Year Outlook). records.text: World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 11 CA rates: Upside risks Katie Craig Ralph Axel BofAS BofAS Themes: CAD rates driven by inflation risk Canadian 2y rates have sold off 70bp since the start of the Iran conflict. Market pricing has largely been driven by moves in oil and expectations for BoC hikes. BoC OIS now implies ~1.75 hikes remaining in ’26. While our economists expect the BoC to remain on hold for the year, we see market pricing now as roughly fair due to hawkish BoC and upside risk to inflation. The move in CAD rates in recent weeks has been driven by inflation risk premium in the form of higher breakevens (nominal rate - real rate). 5y inflation breaks increased from 1.9% at the start of 2026 to 2.3% today, explaining most of the 5y rate increase in this period. The CAD curve bear flattened in March and April but has retraced marginally over May. The 2s10s curve is now 10bp flatter vs Feb month -end. We continue to see the CAD curve steepener vs US flattener as an attractive carry and roll position . Our CAD rates views: On duration: we recently shifted from outright long to neutral due to uncertainty around the oil outlook. On swaps: we like being short front -end swap spreads vs being long in the US to position for tighter funding conditions in CAD vs soft/stable funding in the US. On the curve: we continue to like CAD curve steepeners vs US flatteners. Forecasts: below forwards at the front-end We leave our CAD rates forecasts unchanged despite being below forwards.

If AI can transform 20% of all tasks today, based on recent estimates, and only 23% of those tasks make economic sense to automate, that means less than 5% of tasks would end up being done by AI. If automated tasks, on average, allow for almost 30% reduction in labour costs, the overall savings in labour costs would stand slightly above 1% (1.2%). records.text: han what we're seeing today. Global growth is at 3.5% and AI-driven productivity gains are currently adding 10 basis points per year to it. But in the best case, AI-driven productivity could lift growth by about 1% a year over the next decade, increasing global growth to 4.5%. Innovation productivity is the real multiplier AI can also lift the productivity of innovation itself, speeding up idea generation and improving the growth rate, not just the level, of long-run output. This means that even modest improvements will compound over time into substantially stronger economic outcomes. In our view, there will be significant increases in productivity in the long run, but not just immediately. Diffusion will create winners and losers Countries with stronger capacity to adopt AI, especially the US and China, will capture productivity increases earlier and more fully than potential laggards, such as Europe and EM economies. Even small differences in variables today, like diffusion, could not only drive bigger one-time productivity boosts but also leave some permanently ahead while others fall behind never managing to close an ever-expanding gap. AI will widen the r* divide across global economies Fast adopters (US/China) are likely to see higher neutral interest rates (r*) as stronger productivity boosts the return on investment and drives more demand for capital. records.text: remain medium-term bulls on SEK and forecast EUR/SEK will fall to 10.20 in about 12 months' time, to which markets assign about a 15% probability. SEK has lagged other risk and cyclically sensitive currencies, we think partly reflecting that the rebound in risk assets has not been matched by an increase in global growth expectations. A resumption of global energy supplies could see meaningful SEK 'catch-up' to its risk-sensitive peers like NOK and AUD. This week's labor data showed a m/m tightening in the labor market, which at the margin may bolster expectations for a Riksbank hike before the September meeting. NOK Our view: Bullish Risk skew: Bullish Watch: Unemployment Rate, 1Q GDP We remain bullish on NOK, though we are unconvinced NOK may continue to outperform SEK, particularly once we see clearer evidence of a resumption of energy flows. NOK has proven very attractive to investors given its combined positive forces from strong local growth, a hawkish Norges Bank, high carry, and risk sensitivity. This popularity has resulted in clear long positioning though, which creates asymmetric risk for a pullback. We are also concerned that investors have priced too much for hikes at the June Norges Bank meeting, and weak labor market data or a weak GDP print next week could see the market reduce the 10bp of hikes priced in.

There would be more securities for the short to deliver from the basket, and the long is effectively short a delivery option that increases as switch optionality rises. • Above 6% yield: The CTDs gravitate towards longer-duration securities (longer maturity,• lower coupon) in the basket. These are more sensitive to yield changes, so prices decline more as yields rise and make these securities more economical (cheaper) to deliver. The conversion factors for new bonds entering the deliverable basket would be above 1. Stylized example Figure 4 and Figure 5 show a stylized example of the conversion factor-adjusted price for US and WN futures, assuming flat yield curve scenarios across the deliverable basket. The bonds with the lowest adjusted price at a given yield level is the CTD. At yields well below or above 6%, there is greater dispersion and the CTDs can be readily identified. At around 6%, there is less dispersion and multiple securities can cluster together as close contenders, so CTD switch risk is greatest. However, the example assumes convergence occurs at 6% under a flat yield assumption. In practice, the yield curve is not flat. Figure 6 and Figure 7 take into account the current shape of the yield curve in the deliverable basket and apply parallel shifts. As noted above, intervention warning, and actual intervention, should continue to support the JPY ahead of the 160 line of defense versus the USD. Even so, supply-demand of FX funds for the JPY continue to face persistent JPY selling pressure from Japanese investors’ overseas investment, among other factors, meaning risks are likely to remain skewed toward JPY weakness (see JPY: Post-intervention outlook, 1 May). Stopgap measures through supply-demand support may be able to buy time but this situation differs substantially from the supply-demand-driven market selloff in the first half of last year, when rates rose alongside a marked cheapening in ASW, suggesting that supply-demand improvement alone may not bring a stable market reversal. Given the latent risk of further JPY weakness from additional BoJ purchases (and the associated cost of additional FX intervention), they are unlikely to provide a fundamental solution unless the market comes to recognize fiscal discipline and BoJ rate hikes. In the BoJ’s published measure of US-style core CPI excluding special factors, “education free-of-charge policies” are treated as special factors, but details on which specific items are excluded have not been disclosed. Given that the BoJ’s published US-style core stood at +1.7% YoY for March, we think it is likely that tuition-related items were adjusted, while elementary school lunch fees and nursery school fees, which had not shown large movements previously, were probably not included as special factors ( Exhibit 2 ). However, from the April release onward, we think these items are also likely to be included as special factors. In that case, the BoJ's March US-style core CPI excluding special factors would be revised upward to +1.8% YoY, while the April figure would likely remain largely unchanged at +1.7% YoY. We maintain our expectation of a rate hike at the June meeting. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 3 BoE: hikes in July and September We now expect the BoE to hike in July and September (vs June and July before) to 4.25%, with risks of one hike as before. A softer gas profile than we were expecting, dovish inflation/labour market data and lack of explicit guidance on June from the BoE in recent weeks make us delay the timing of hikes. We still think the BoE is likely to hike twice (with risks of one) in coming months to guard against second-round effects. There are a few risks to our call. June can't be fully ruled out, but risks in our view are tilted to further delays. Moreover, as with the ECB, perhaps even more so, we think the risk of the BoE looking through the shock is higher than the risk of more than 50bps of hikes. We continue to expect quarterly cuts from Q2 2027 to 3.5% by end-2027. After the PMIs is pretty much before the PMIs (or the reverse) Going back to the data, this week’s “flash” PMI print featured as a potential trigger for ECB repricing in some client discussions. Half a day after the release, markets are still quite firmly pricing two hikes by September. We don’t agree with the principle. First, the PMI print is compatible with our ECB call. Second, qualitatively, the PMI signal isn’t that surprising (higher input prices, lower demand, lower output, weaker employment). We think the discussion around this topic will remain in focus for the rest of the year, and we continue to think that the order of operations around balance sheet reduction will be key. In this note we discuss the factors that have contributed to the growth in the Fed’s assets and liabilities over time, and the evolution of the Fed’s footprint in markets. We then summarize our baseline path for the Fed’s balance sheet and what that implies for the Fed’s presence in the Treasury market, before considering what could alter the balance sheet trajectory over time. We expect only modest expansion in the Fed’s balance sheet until early 2027, after which we anticipate a return to a more trend-like growth of $300bn per year to keep reserves steady around 11% of bank assets. While there are downside risks to this baseline, just keeping the balance sheet stable would likely see reserves steadily decline at a modest pace in outright terms and more swiftly as a share of bank assets. Given the uncertain runway, likely limited impact on the Fed’s ability to lower rates, and potential costs of overshooting, we think the bar is high to a meaningful reduction in the size of the balance sheet. Factors behind the growth and the evolution of reserve demand Since the middle of 2008, the Fed’s balance sheet has grown by $5.8tn, rising from 6.4% of GDP to about 21% today with a peak near 36% in 2022. Expansion of securities holdings is responsible for the entirety of the point-to-point growth in Fed assets. In this case, based on past demand patterns, the interest would need to appear considerably higher than the yield on the 5y bond. For the super-long sector, we think a fixed interest rate product is appropriate. This is because there is already a variable-rate 10y bond. If the fixed interest were in line with the market, we think there could be considerable demand. However, in this case the one-year lockup period would be a problem, as it would be too short. If, for example, if the period is extended to five years and assuming a 30y bond at 4%, an investor would receive four years of coupons over five years, earnings an annual return over five years of around 3.2% (here we ignore the discount factor). This would mean a yield around 100bp higher than fixed-rate 5y JGBs for individual investors, causing a distortion in the system. It would simply increase the cost to the MoF, while also affecting corporate bonds for individual investors. While higher yields will definitely stimulate demand, the interest rate will not likely be set too high. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

As we mentioned in our last weekly (see US Rates Weekly - Global buyers strike?), there are no signs of pass- through into core inflation yet. Core services inflation excluding shelter and energy driven airfares inflation continued to decrease in April and so did core goods inflation. If shelter inflation, which is 44% of core index, continues to decline and eventually falls below 3%, even with some pass through of higher energy prices into core goods (24% of core index), we find it very hard to justify > 3% core inflation in 2026, which is already being priced by the market. As we show in Figure 6, the increase in 2026 headline inflation expectations since the start of this month have outpaced the expected increase in gasoline prices (based on the December gasoline futures contract price). This shows that markets are pricing increased pass through of energy prices into core components of the inflation basket. While we do agree that there will be some impact of higher energy prices on core, in our view, they are already sufficiently priced in the market. Figure 4. PEP made news this week with Bloomberg reporting that single-serve bags would see price increases in June between ~4%-7%. However, this follows PEP's Feb announcement to reduce prices by as much as 15% on key larger SKUs (8oz and above), all of which add confusion. 22 May 2026 Equity Global Thomas (T.J.) Median short-term inflation expectations have increased notably, while long-term expectations have moved little. Looking at the distribution of expectations, the latest Survey of Professional n Forecasters (SPF) also shows that the right tail of short-term expectations has fattened notably. The distribution around long-term expectations, however, has remained anchored around 2% with a broadly unchanged distribution. Market expectations have shifted more materially towards pricing higher inflation at all horizons. Across countries, we find that short-term expectations in the ECB’s Consumer n Expectations Survey (CES) have moved up throughout the Euro area, with consumers in smaller Southern countries reporting the biggest increases. Across income groups, we see that most of the move higher in expectations has been driven by lower earners who also report lower growth expectations, pointing to some stagflationary concerns. Taken together, the recent inflation expectations data point to a material rise in n short-term expectations—with concerns around further upside risks—consistent with significant direct and indirect inflation effects from the energy shock. For the full publication, including the appendices, please see the original publication. US CPI inflation swap total return trackers Tracking the performance of an inflation swap position with precision is more complicated than simply measuring the change in spot rates from trade initiation to closure. While that can be a reasonable proxy much of the time, base effects alone can distort spot performance meaningfully even if the market-implied index level at maturity (which is what actually dictates performance) is unchanged. A more precise analysis needs to isolate the shift in the inflation curve, holding the effective and maturity dates constant for the life of the trade, while properly accounting for the discount rate (which matters for the net present value of the cash flow at maturity). records.text: M Idea 2 13F - Quarter over Quarter We aggregated all available 13F reports for the quarter ending March 31st, with the filing period ending May 15th. Below, we summarize our key findings to help investors assess how positioning has shifted over the last quarter. Please note that these holdings reflect positions as of March 31st, and allocations may have changed since reporting. Additionally, the majority of filers are long-only funds, with ~5% of assets represented by hedge funds. 13F data is limited to long equity positions and does not include derivative or short-side exposures. Our analysis focuses on the top 100 funds by AUM and the top 100 hedge funds by AUM. Q1 saw investors add to Energy (+1.5%) and Industrials (+0.8%) and sell Financials (- 1.4%) and Communication Services (-0.8%) (Exhibit 1 ). The S&P 500 fell -4.6% in Q1 with Energy (+37%) as the top sector on the back of the US/Iran conflict so it was no surprise that Energy was a top gainer in active share. The other sectors that also gained active share also saw positive returns during the quarter. Hedge funds saw a similar trend with Energy (+1.3%), Industrials (+0.9%) and Utilities (+0.3%) as the top sectors. Hedge funds also added to all sectors that saw positive Q1 returns with the exception of Staples where HFs trimmed positions by -0.4% active share. records.text: Under those same assumptions for growth in currency, the TGA, and bank assets, reserves as a share of bank assets would stabilize around 11% versus the 11.5-12% range seen recently. Reserves as a share of bank assets would drop by about 4pp (1.2pp per year on average) by the end of the decade under an unchanged balance sheet size. A return to a $20bn per month pace of balance sheet reduction would correspond to a 7pp decline (2pp per year on average; Exhibit 9). Our baseline for RMPs combined with the reinvestment MBS runoff into USTs implies a monthly pace of UST purchases of $20-to-25bn in the near term and $35-to-40bn in the steady state. Given funding needs implied by our economists’ deficit projections, Fed UST holdings as a share of the overall market would rise by about 1pp to about 15.3% by the end of the decade, still firmly below the pre-GFC average. If the Fed kept its balance sheet stable and adhered to the policy of reinvesting MBS runoff into USTs, the Fed’s share of total USTs would fall a bit more than 1pp to near 13% by the end of the decade. And a return to balance sheet runoff via MBS (i.e. UST holdings unchanged) would see that share fall 3pp to 11.3% (Exhibit 10). The mood towards Brazil remains constructive (see also our previous report, Brazil: the new gold? ). Investors we met were not concerned about the recent underperformance of Brazilian assets, and some mentioned that they have room to add risk depending on the evolution of the external backdrop. Investors continue to struggle as the headline volatility regarding the war remains high. Some mentioned that the market appears to be willing to ignore some of the headlines, but they are waiting for more clarity about the war before adding more directional positions. Several factors have been driving interest in allocations across Brazilian assets. Those include being a large supplier of commodities, being geographically far from the conflict, having big reserves of rare earth minerals, having a clean electricity matrix favoring potential investments in data centers, among others. Activity is showing some resilience March's industrial production (IP) increased 0.1% momsa , down from +0.9% in February. The print was above expectations (BofA: - 0.9%, consensus: -0.1%). records.text: M Update 4 CAD Our view: Neutral Risk skew: Neutral Watch: Payroll Employment Change – SEPH, Quarterly GDP Annualized We are neutral on USD/CAD after CPI surprised to the downside relative to market expectations. We think CAD remains caught between two opposing forces: a soft domestic growth backdrop and the increasing likelihood that CAD could benefit from a less-backwardated Brent Oil curve should markets begin pricing higher-for-longer oil prices. We explored here how a flatter oil curve at elevated oil prices implies USD/CAD weakness, but note this relationship broke down somewhat post-2015. Since the US has increased oil exports and China has decreased oil imports significantly, this shape has not appeared yet, as noted by our commodity strategists. Until then, USD/CAD could grind higher as markets continue to price hikes out of the GoC curve. AUD Our view: Neutral Risk skew: Bullish Watch: CPI, Household Spending We maintain our bullish skew on AUD, as the longer-term AUD outlook has improved and positioning has shifted to slightly short. RBA pricing is now close to our economists’ expectation. And after a downside labor market surprise, AUD positioning has normalized to just below the 50th percentile – below NZD, JPY, and NOK. The AUD-bullish case is also supported by APRA data suggesting superannuation funds reduced notional FX derivative positions, ongoing immigration inflows, and rising public-sector spending as a share of GDP . records.text: US Rates Weekly 22 May 2026 Citi Research 4 Overview: Et tu, Waller? What anchors Treasuries after decoupling from oil? Last week we were forced to move to tactically neutral, given the lack of near-term bullish catalysts, although we reiterated our lower YE26 forecasts (see US Rates Weekly - Global buyers strike?). Indeed, seasonals are not especially clear as we enter June, but yields do tend to cap out and move lower as the summer progresses (Figure 4). This week yields may have hit a light resistance level, but they remain attractive relative to Dec26 WTI futures (Figure 5). We find the yield/oil divergence at this juncture somewhat puzzling as WTI appears locally capped at around $100- $110/barrel with the current backdrop of the Strait of Hormuz. Thus, we see somewhat limited risks for oil to realize at levels higher than forwards by year-end, although clearly there remains mark-to-market risks. That risk is important, as we see two stories to push yields materially higher from here: 1) a multiple-round hiking cycle (> 3 hikes), which presumably requires 3.5% core PCE on a consistent basis, and/or 2) a sharp increase in term premium. Note: Futures trading involves substantial risk of loss. On inflation, forwards are pricing in a materially overstated view of core CPI, in our view. Source: Federal Reserve, Barclays Research Against this backdrop, we expect the Fed to dial RMPs down further, likely pausing them full stop at the mid-June calendar update until mid-September when it moves back to a steady state level of $20bn/m ( Figure 1). This would keep the nominal size of the balance sheet broadly stable, as ongoing T-bill purchases would continue to replace maturing MBS. However, we would not rule out its staying at zero for even longer, and it is not obvious that this alone would be sufficient to lift money market rates back toward IORB, particularly if the reserve demand curve has indeed flattened materially. While the path of the TGA and reserves have material swings on a day-to-day basis, our forecast for the months ahead suggests that reserves should average above levels that prevailed in February, even with no further RMPs ( Figure 4 and Figure 5). That, in turn, raises the possibility that the Fed may need to keep RMPs at zero through the end of the year. The possibility of larger declines in reserve demand is already sparking discussions about potentially restarting quantitative tightening down the road, if ending RMPs alone is not enough. This could entail allowing MBS to roll off without replacement or permitting some Treasury redemptions to go unreplaced. 21 May 2026 22 Barclays | Glob

records.text: World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 31 Philippines: Inflation gathering pace Jojo Gonzales Abhay Gupta Philippine Equity Partners Merrill Lynch (Singapore) April inflation shocked even more; rate hikes forthcoming The Consumer Pirce Index (CPI) rose 7.2% YoY in April, well outside the 5.6 -6.4% range estimated by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). This is the second straight month inflation was worse than the forecast range of the BSP. The upward price pressure c ame mainly from Rice (+13.7% YoY), Electricity (+16.9%), and Transport (+21.4%). Core inflation too accelerated to 3.9% YoY, suggesting that price pressure may be spreading beyond the more volatile food and fuel factors. The April inflation print reinforces our view that the BSP will hike policy rates at its next two meetings, in June and August, by 25bp each meeting. We believe inflation will peak in 4Q26, just shy of double-digit rates. This ciritcally assumes our baseline FY26E scenario of Brent averaging US$92.5/bbl, compared to US$87 average YTD and US$110 spot. Despite growing expectations of policy rate hikes by the BSP, the peso depreciated to new all-time lows, touching P61.72/$ through late May. Strategy – Twin deficits expose PHP to oil price shock PHP’s wide twin deficits increase its vulnerability to the ongoing oil price shock. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 34 there would be little to gain from waiting for more data by September. However, +50bp (to 2.5%) is likely sufficient unless the severe scenario comes into play (at present, oil prices are close to the adverse scenario, but gas is in line with the baseline). Much will depend on the openness of the Strait of Hormuz, but the current base case is that the ECB is unlikely to deliver 75bp+ of hikes, as is currently priced, not least given looming demand destruction. In our forecasts, this reflects via a slight bullish bias for the front-end for H2, but it is only marginal. The main message is a range-bound view, and we stick with 3% 10yr Bund for year-end, with a modest steepening bias. As for EMU spreads, the near-term outlook is still dependent on broader risk sentiment with little idiosyncratic event risk. We stick the view that spreads are likely to remain a little wider than pre-conflict given the prospect for ECB hikes and a weaker growth outlook that challenges deficit progress. Further fiscal responses to the conflict are also possible. We also note that the share of EGB issuance in H2 is likely to be a little higher than last year. records.text: In Figure 18, we report a regression between SOFR/IORB and our preferred front- end heuristic, private T -bill outstanding minus bank reserves. records.text: 6 Global Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 Special factors When thinking about the labor market outlook for 2026 and 2027, it is important to take into account a few factors: the upcoming World Cup, summer weakness in jobs, the supply shock from tighter immigration policies and its impact on breakven job growth, and risks of QCEW-driven payroll revisions. i) World Cup effect: temporary, modest boost The 2026 FIFA World Cup (June-July) is likely to provide a temporary lift to payrolls, particularly in leisure & hospitality, trade & transportation, construction and professional & business services. Some headline estimates suggest ~185k jobs could be added. However, several factors will likely limit the measured immediate impact on payrolls: i) a significant portion of demand will likely be met via overtime (which does not increase payrolls), rather than temporary hiring, ii) independent contractor usage (e.g., security, logistics) is not captured in the Establishment survey, and iii) regular visitors are expected to avoid host cities (tourism substitution), and this would offset some of the boost from the World Cup. Looking at Copa America 2024, roughly one-quarter the scale of the World Cup in terms of attendance, we saw no discernible impact on national payrolls. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 28 Saudi Arabia The kingdom’s 1Q budget outturn has drawn considerable attention, as market participants look for early evidence of the conflict’s fiscal impact. Our analysis suggests that the fiscal accounts had likely begun to drift from the FY26 plan before the conflict, which has further compounded the slippage. The 1Q’26 deficit of SAR125.7bn absorbed roughly three-quarters of the full-year envelope (SAR165bn) in a single quarter, driven mainly by spending against broadly flat revenues. Looking ahead, we expect the conflict and the Hormuz closure to reshape the picture in three respects. First, pipeline-constrained export volumes are likely to limit the revenue benefit from sharply higher oil prices. Second, defense, infrastructure repair and subsidy outlays should generate additional spending pressures from 2Q’26. Third, the FY26 budget framework, formulated under pre-war assumptions, will likely require recalibration as the new environment takes shape. Our base case envisages a budget deficit of 5.7% of GDP this year, broadly unchanged from 2025 (5.8%), with wide confidence intervals reflecting the uncertain geopolitical backdrop. South Africa We downgrade our real GDP growth forecast again slightly, to 1.1% for 2026 given the ongoing Middle East supply side shock. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 21 May 2026 5 Simple arithmetic shows the limit today The discussion above shows how estimated effects of AI on productivity systematically shrink as we move from micro towards macro. There are several potential reasons for this. At the task level, tasks are well defined. As complexity increases, AI must integrate with the workflow and the organization, workers need to acquire the skills, plus technical, legal, and organizational constraints can slow or reduce the impact (data protection, security concerns, among many others, are also natural sand in the wheel for adoption rates). This is even more the case at the macro level, where diffusion can be even slower given all the constraints cited above. There are also well-established potential measurement issues that could magnify the gap between micro and macro effects. Those include, among others, from poor measurement of improvements in outcomes such as quality, reallocation effects, non- linearities in the impact of AI, or distorted measurement of intangible investments. There are also physical constraints that could slow AI’s scaling (energy, infrastructure, which could also be relevant for the long-run impact), as these factors will help determine the transition of micro efficiency gains into macro productivity. We have noted recently that in the US, price elasticity of demand is ~7% (demand declines 7% when prices go up by 100%, all else equal). In the case of civil aviation, the elasticity is even less. records.text: While the Fed’s holdings of Treasuries have risen meaningfully in outright terms and as a share of GDP , the increase in Fed holdings has not outpaced growth of the broader Treasury market over the last 20 years. The Fed’s UST holdings currently represent about 14% of USTs outstanding versus a pre-GFC average of about 17% (Exhibit 2). The more notable shift in footprint has occurred in the agency MBS market, where pre-2008 the Fed held nothing and now accounts for about 22% of the overall market (Exhibit 3). While the process is a gradual one, Fed officials have long maintained a goal to return to a Treasury-only portfolio, with the current policy to reinvest proceeds from the MBS roll-off into Treasury bills. Two major liabilities sit largely outside of the Fed’s control—the TGA and currency in circulation. The TGA ’s growth reflects a shift in Treasury policy alongside an increase in day-to-day cash needs. Up to the GFC, Treasury held the bulk of its cash with depository institutions (see here for an overview) before shifting to keeping all of its cash at the Fed in the TGA. In 2015, Treasury established a policy to maintain a cash balance in the TGA sufficient to cover one week of projected outflows. records.text: M Global Idea 2 and triple 2024 levels. The more remarkable point is not just the scale. It is that this acceleration is happening despite rising costs. From copper to gas turbines to memory, large price increases in key components have done little to dent AI enthusiasm. There’s a term for demand that’s relatively insensitive to price: inelasticity. You often find it in things that are essential (electricity) or deeply desired (concert tickets). In the case of AI investment, it may be both, with companies eager to shape what they see as the next big technology of the future, and also worried about falling behind if they don't. For such an important long-term investment, inelasticity extends to the cost of financing it. We have seen record issuance from technology firms in 2026, even as yields have moved higher. Because such a program pulls forward replacement demand for consumer durable goods, a payback effect would eventually emerge, as households will not replace cars, home appliances, and smartphones every year. For example, home appliance sales growth dropped from +53% yoy last May to -15% yoy this April. The policy change to the auto purchase tax has exacerbated the slowdown in auto sales this year. To support the adoption of electric vehicles (EVs), the government exempted the 10% purchase tax on EVs in previous years. With EV share of auto sales exceeding that of internal combustion engine (ICE) cars, the purchase tax on EVs was raised from 0% to 5% this year, leading to a notable decline in EV and total auto sales. According to China Passenger Car Association data, domestic auto sales volume growth declined from +16% yoy in Q2 last year to -18% yoy in Q1 this year. CTD switches are relevant for the US (classic bond) and WN (ultra bond) Treasury futures contract. At higher rates, the CTD is likely to switch to a higher-duration security. The CTD typically switches to a longer-maturity security in US and to a shorter-maturity one in the case of WN. This is because the deliverable baskets exhibit different duration profiles ( Figure 3). In the US contract, longer-maturity bonds have higher duration, while in WN, shorter-maturity bonds do. The steady increase in rates over the past couple of years has resulted in 30y bonds' being issued at higher coupons, while the ones issued at low coupons (1-2%) are still in the WN basket. Rebalancing needs Since 2023, asset managers' gross long positions in US and WN have increased about 30% and 80%, respectively (per open interest data from CFTC). The empirical DV01 of the US futures contract, which measures the sensitivity of price changes to yield changes in the deliverable basket, has been trading at about 14, which is close to the shortest-duration securities. A 50-60bp sell-off could switch the CTD to the longest-duration security in the 2050 sector, which implies about $40mn 01 of rebalancing needs in AM gross long positions. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 22 China China's growth momentum slowed sharply in April. Both supply and demand indicators missed expectations by a wide margin, hitting or approaching post- Covid lows. Industrial production grew just 4.1%YoY despite upbeat exports, hitting the lowest since mid-2023. Retail sales rose a mere 0.2%YoY in April, a new low since 2023 and cumulative FAI turned negative at -1.6%YoY Ytd, implying a month rate of -8.0%YoY per our estimate. With the beat in both CPI and PPI, real growth could be negative for retail sales and close to -10%YoY for investment. Domestic weakness was revealed further and Mideast conflict impact surfaced. Reduced trade-in subsidies knocked roughly 2ppts off headline retail sales; infrastructure investment turned negative at -3.0%YoY in April, and property investment deteriorated despite green shoots. On Mideast impact, direct supply- side disruptions were limited: output of petrochemical products recorded a small contraction in April (ethylene: -4.1%YoY; sulfuric acid: -2.2%YooY). Secondary demand effects via export channels were barely visible, though elevated prices and heightened uncertainty did weigh on domestic consumption and capex. Stagflation risks are rising. Headline figures, especially in nominal terms, should hold up on the back of the PPI beat. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 3 Fiscal policy is the elephant in the room A natural question is whether a potential inability of the Fed to hike amid political pressure could lead to higher inflation expectations. But that is not the case, as the selloff in the back end has been driven by real rates, not breakevens (Exhibit 2). The market still believes in the Fed fulfilling its mandates. In our view, this means that the ever-worsening fiscal dynamics in the US are a key driver of the selloff. Term premium in real rates is reflective of higher fiscal risks. In an environment where Fed could potentially be on the table and become a driver of even larger fiscal deficits amid rising debt servicing costs, the long end of the curve becomes more sensitive to what should be primarily a move in short-end rates. Things can take longer to happen but happen faster than expected We have long argued that the US economy didn’t need rate cuts (even when we thought they would still be delivered) and have also argued that a tightening in financial and liquidity conditions was the Achilles heel of asset prices. The war and reflation risks are triggering that tightening amid the pervasive fiscal dynamics we have long highlighted. The question is not so much whether the Fed should hike, but rather if it will be able to do so amid political pressure shall the fundamentals really ask for it. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 27 Turkey Market focus centered on the April rate decision and the May Inflation Report (IR). As expected, the CBT kept its policy rate unchanged at 37% in the April MPC meeting. We believe that the CBT's decision to hold the policy rate rather than align it with the average funding rate signals a wait-and-see stance in the near-term. Turning to the May IR, the governor’s presentation was framed around one dominant theme: the supply shock from the Middle East conflict and the Strait of Hormuz closure. In our view, two signals stood out. First, the new forecasts assume policy stays tighter for longer than envisaged in the previous Report. Second, in a structural shift, the CBT will abandon forecast-band communication in favor of baseline point forecasts paired with a narrative risk assessment. Against this backdrop, we expect the CBT to keep rates on hold at the next MPC meeting, barring renewed pressures on reserves. Looking beyond June, we expect the room for easing in 2H to be more limited than the consensus view suggests, with the policy rate ending the year at 35%, versus the consensus of about 32%; if anything, the risks to our forecast are titled toward a tighter stance. records.text: Global Credit Trader: Rates (still) in the driver’s seat Outlining a hypothetical scenario for (lower) full-year total returns In early April, we refreshed our total return forecasts for the USD and EUR corporate credit markets, across IG and HY. In addition to reflecting our expectation for moderately wider spreads, the total return forecasts also incorporated our rates strategists’ forecasts for global rates markets. The key takeaway (at the time) was that total returns would likely rank in ‘the middle of the pack’ vs. the past three decades. Since that time, global bond yields have risen meaningfully (Exhibit 2). As our rates strategy colleagues have noted, the drivers across the various regions (US, UK, Europe) have been multifaceted, reflecting varying degrees of inflation risk premium, political risk premium, and even some growth optimism. Our US rates strategists’ baseline forecast calls for lower US yields over time, led by the 2yr-5yr part of the curve. That said, they have also acknowledged that the case for lower yields in the near term is likely to remain a difficult one, absent (for example) a resolution to the Iran conflict. For corporate credit investors, we see two clear implications. First and foremost, there is a mathematical headwind to full-year 2026 total returns. There is general agreement with our view that higher oil prices should pose a headwind to the consumer, but not change the trajectory of the US economy, where growth in economic activity continues to be supported by AI-related business spending, healthy upper-income household balance sheets, and loose fiscal policy. We have received little push-back around our forecast for growth in real GDP (2.3% and 2.6% 4Q/4Q in 2026 and 2027) and our outlook for a stable labor market with some improvement in labor demand. There are always differences in degree, but there is agreement in the resiliency of the US economy. Questions remain about 1) further fiscal stimulus ahead of the midterms, 2) the outcome of Section 232 and 301 trade investigations, and 3) the pending review of the USMCA trade agreement. On net, investors are inclined to think the bar for further stimulus is high, a push on tariffs ahead of the midterms where affordability is a key issue is unlikely, and substantive changes in the USMCA are low probability. Macro gains are lagging micro so far AI is already boosting productivity gains in very specific well-defined tasks (i.e., +55% in software development, +40% in writing). But these increases have yet to scale sharply across the whole economy. In practice, slow adoption, skills gaps, and organizational constraints have limited AI's impact on output. Thus, for now, economy-wide productivity (TFP) is only rising about 0.1% per year. This is a small aggregate effect relative to all the excitement around AI. Productivity upside could be 10x the current estimates AI differs from earlier technologies in that it can take on a broader range of tasks and continuously expand what it can do. As AI models improve and the technology spreads to more tasks and becomes cheaper, macro gains could be much larger. We think AI could have a much bigger impact on aggregate productivity-up to 10x larger than what we're seeing today. records.text: ab 22 May 2026 Global Research US Daily Data Recap Waller backs removing easing bias There was another repricing in rates markets this morning, with Governor Waller adding his name to the list of FOMC participants on board with removing the easing bias from the policy statement. He stated that on the basis of the recent labor market and inflation data, he would support statement language that makes it "clear that a rate cut is no more likely in the future than a rate increase." He stated that he was prepared to be patient in holding policy at its current restrictive setting, and that rate hikes would be premature at this point, but rate cuts would require improvement in inflation or a "significant deterioration" in the labor market. Adding to the remarks from Governor Waller, longer-run inflation expectations revised up 0.5 pp to 3.9% in the final May University of Michigan survey, back to a level last seen in October 2025. Short-run expectations have been pushing higher with the surge in gasoline prices and revised up 0.3 pp to 4.8% in the final May data, but remain below last year's peak in May (6.6%). Sentiment continues to test historical records, registering a series low of 44.8 in May. Kevin Warsh's swearing-in ceremony to his roles as Chair and Governor of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System took place this morning, where he gave brief remarks. Rates Strategy Shinichiro Kadota BSJL, Japan | Ayao Ehara BSJL, Japan This week: Yields surge, but rise pauses temporarily following 20y JGB auction This week saw JGB yields rise sharply through the middle of the week before partially declining. The curve bear-steepened in maturities of 10 years and shorter, while showing downward convexity further out, centered around the 30y sector, as yields rose slightly beyond the 10y but fell in the 30y. At the start of the week, the curve bear-steepened at the outset, driven by strong inflation concerns and weak BoJ buying operations. On the 18th, Reuters reported the possibility of the government issuing deficit-financing JGBs to fund a supplementary budget, which further intensified the bear-steepening. Yields continued to rise on the 19th ahead of the 20y auction, but turned lower on the 20th, and the 20y auction cleared smoothly. Amid thin liquidity, yields drifted somewhat lower afterward. For the week as a whole, however, the curve bear-steepened in maturities of 10y and shorter, while the superlong sector was mixed, with 20y and 40y yields slightly higher and 30y yields lower. Inflation heading above 3%, but falling back close to 2% in 2028 – We nudged our inflation forecasts slightly higher again, with headline HICP now averaging 3.0% in 2026 and returning to 2.0% on average only in 2028. records.text: rterly cuts by mid-2027 (also June), probably taking policy rates below 2%. But there are many risks to that call. First, a hold in June, while far from our base case, still has some decent probability. Indeed, a sequence of signs suggesting non-linear adjustments in activity as potentially suggested by French PMIs this week could open the door to a June hold. We are not there yet and we are unlikely to get enough datapoints, but the door is not closed for the ECB to stay put. This is consistent with our long-held view that the risk of no hikes at all is larger than the risk of more than 50bp of hikes in total. Second, yes, our base case has two hikes in June and July of this year. But the second could slip to September if the data deteriorates faster than expected and energy prices behave a bit better. A June+July sequence requires a sense of urgency. Finally, the central bank could start reversing the 2026 hikes a little earlier than we expect, although they will probably want to see firm evidence of inflation (including core) being past peak with no tangible second-round effects on 2027 wage growth. That said, like in 2025/26, we could see a pause at a 2% deposit rate until a persistent undershoot eventually pushes them into cuts below 2% in 2028.

We see further tailwinds from higher AUD yields, resilient US equities, and a broadly weaker dollar (especially vs Asia FX). We expect higher oil and gas prices will also provide modest support for AUD although the impact will be limited in the absence of new mining capex. We continue to expect AUD to reach 0.74 by Q4 ’26 before easing to around 0.73, consistent with our view that the RBA will begin cutting rates in late 2027. Upside risks: positive AUD carry, commodities strength, USD weakness boosts AU super fund hedge ratios. Downside risks: crowded AUD longs. RBA monetary policy to remain restrictive Inflation risks remain skewed to the upside given the higher starting point for inflation in Australia and supply disruptions in the Middle East. While a cash rate above 4.35% cannot be ruled out, our economists expect the RBA to remain on hold until restrictive policy is ultimately unwound in 2H ‘27. Overall, Australia is likely to have the highest policy rate among G10 central banks, which should underpin AUD strength alongside a weaker dollar. Yields initially rose after reports that Iran intended to retain enriched uranium domestically, pushing Brent crude briefly back above $107/bbl and lifting front-end yields (2y: +5bp intraday to 4.11%; 10y: +3bp intraday to 4.61%). Risk sentiment later stabilized after reports suggesting US-Iran negotiations had “narrowed the gaps,” allowing crude prices to reverse lower and Treasury yields to retrace most of the move (2y: +2.2bp; 10y: -1.8bp; 30y: -3.0bp). The curve flattened modestly as front-end yields remained pressured by persistent inflation concerns and hawkish Fed commentary. US activity data continued to point to relative economic resilience, with May manufacturing PMI rising to 55.3 versus 53.8 expected, while services activity softened modestly to 50.9 and the Philadelphia Fed index unexpectedly fell into contraction territory at -0.4. The $19bn 10-year TIPS reopening tailed by nearly 2bp at 2.169%, reflecting continued investor caution around inflation and supply absorption. • Fed commentary maintained a firm inflation focus as policymakers continued emphasizing the risks associated with repeated supply shocks and elevated energy prices. What we feel strongly about is the following: If there is a resolution of the conflict and oil prices move back below $100/barrel, the global economy seems likely to land on its feet. Growth this year will be a little lower and headline inflation somewhat higher as a result of the disruptions, but overall economic performance should remain solid. The question that we continue to grapple with is whether similarly solid performance could accrue if oil prices remain above $100/barrel. Our baseline view is that growth would fall appreciably. But, as noted above, the global economy has shown surprising resilience since the onset of the conflict and, more broadly, has shaken off a variety of shocks in the years since the pandemic. In 2022, it was Russia-Ukraine; in 2023 and 2024, it was central bank rate hikes; and last year it was President Trump’s tariffs. In each case, growth has continued in the neighborhood of trend. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 22/05/2026 14:34:12 GMT Distributed on: 22/05/2026 14:34:12 GMT 22 May 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Europe United Kingdom Economics UK Weekly Digest Date 'Manchesterism': What The Bond Sell- Off Told Us About Potential Issuance As the UK local election results rang out, market fears around a potential shift in Government increased dramatically. By Monday (11 May), markets were reacting to the possibility of a major shift in politics – including the fiscal outlook. Questions around the fiscal framework picked up and, accordingly, questions around more borrowing also increased. Tracing the gilt moves through the temporary sell off Following the local elections, bond markets started to price in some element of political risk. On 11 May, 10y bond yields shot up 9bps. On 12 May, 10y yields were up a further 10bps. By the 15 May, 10y bond yields were up a cumulative 26bps. 30y gilt yields were up 27bps over the same weekly period. On both accounts, gilt yields were back to levels not seen in decades – with growth showing few signs of resurgence. Put simply, market moves were perhaps not just a reflection of global moves, but an assessment of future borrowing uncertainty. The latest SPF results indicate that the short-term expectations distribution has become less symmetric, with the probability mass (along with the mean) shifting notably to the right: the probability of inflation being higher than 2.8% in three quarters’ time rose from 10% in 2025 to 46% in 2026Q2 (Exhibit 2, left). The distribution around long-term expectations, however, has remained anchored around 2% with broadly unchanged density, suggesting little upside risk for the long-term outlook for now. Market expectations have shifted more notably towards pricing higher inflation. The distribution of implied probability of inflation outcomes, derived from options pricing, has shifted to the right and shown a more notable widening of the right tail across the horizons, suggesting increased hedging and higher inflation risk premium across the curve (Exhibit 2, right). records.text: The second takeaway relates to the cross-market comparison between USD and EUR IG. The outperformance of USD vs. EUR has been much more visible in cash spreads than in synthetic indices. In our view, this is largely because the supply backdrop has been much more supportive in the USD cash market (Exhibit 9). We continue to retain a bias toward owning USD spreads vs. EUR spreads, but tactically the divergence between cash and synthetic markets suggests a better re-entry point may come after some normalization in the issuance calendar. The third takeaway is in the leveraged loan market, where the strong technical tailwind has propped up loan prices higher than the fundamental picture might convey (Exhibit 10). The mix of less borrower-friendly monetary policy, an overhang related to Software sector disintermediation concerns, and a relatively elevated near-term maturity wall have all been subdued as investors are driven to deploy cash. With the pipeline of future loan supply firmly negative since early this year, the price impact has been relatively muted (Exhibit 11). TATA Steel (TATAIN): Resilient India operations, but caution on European turnaround TATAIN reported a 13% and 50% y/y increase in sales and EBITDA, respectively in 4Q FY26; these were achieved on a 5% y/y increase in sales volumes, particularly in the India markets, and from higher sales prices. India operations remained TATAIN’s key earnings driver, with steel deliveries of 6.2mt (+14% y/y) representing TATAIN’s best-ever quarter. At a consolidated level, the EBITDA increase was partly offset by higher energy and raw material costs, particularly for coking coal, which remains TATAIN’s largest cost driver. Steel-making is inherently raw-material intensive, with 60% of its costs incurred till the hot metal stage, 70% of which is from coking coal, underscoring the structural coal dependency of blast-furnace operations and high sensitivity of margins to coal-price swings. Notably, TATAIN met about 25% of its clean-coal requirement through its captive mines (two open-cast pits in West Bokaro and two underground collieries in Jharia, India), with the balance sourced externally. records.text: free float—the stock of Treasuries outstanding held by non-Fed buyers—would typically bias longer-term yields higher and push swap spreads tighter. However, changes to bank regulation that increase intermediation and/or absorption capacity can help to mitigate those effects. Further, assuming Treasury accounts for the equilibrium size of the Fed’s balance sheet when deciding its composition of issuance—considering the debt ultimately held by the public—it should adapt to a smaller equilibrium Fed balance sheet size/level of reserves by issuing more bills/short-term debt to the public, dampening the impact of a smaller Fed balance sheet on longer term interest rates. Outlook: Inflation set to re-accelerate We expect inflation to re-accelerate going forward. The trajectory of core inflation will be heavily influenced by two main factors: (1) trends in crude oil prices, and (2) government energy price subsidy policies, specifically the extension of gasoline subsidies and the potential reinstatement of electricity and gas subsidies. Our house view assumes that crude oil prices will decline below $80 per barrel by the end of the year. However, considering current price movements, this assumption may be somewhat low. We will incorporate any revisions to our house view into our inflation forecast as they occur. Regarding government policy, we are currently factoring in an extension of gasoline subsidies but have not priced in the resumption of electricity and gas subsidies. We plan to update our forecast as these policies become clearer. We forecast that the core-core inflation rate, which is not directly affected by these factors, will accelerate to around +3.5% in the first half of next year. Year-over-year energy inflation will likely increase further to 11.9%yoy from 10.8%yoy in April, although uncertainty remains high. Our estimates suggest that seasonally adjusted sequential core inflation will tick down to 0.23%mom in May, after printing at 0.25%mom in April (as we do not include the Easter adjustment). This reflects a decline in sequential core goods inflation to 0.09%mom and a sideways move for core services. The surge in energy prices in light of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East has had a notable impact on our inflation forecast. We see core inflation at a weak 2.5%yoy in 2026, rising to 2.7%yoy in 2027Q2 before gradually declining to 2.0%yoy in 2028Q4, above the ECB staff March projections. records.text: E M – L O CA L E YE S F O R A G L O B A L V IEW 221/05/2026 To reiterate, Japan did indeed see import prices climb during the period in question, but initially domestic price hikes were not as hectic as those seen overseas owing to the comparatively slow pace of economic reopening, relatively contained supply-side disruptions and grounded inflation expectations. However, ultimately, this zero-inflation ‘deadlock’ ended up being broken by the yen’s sharp depreciation from spring 2022 that put enormous upward pressure on JPY- denominated import prices and effectively forced domestic firms to start hiking their business-to-business prices (as they continued to do into 2023). The initial catalysts for Japan’s emergence from a zero- inflation world were thus rising energy and food prices coupled with yen depreciation (with a second wave of inflation later hitting from 2024 in what has come to be known as the Reiwa Rice Crisis). Petrochemical prices rising much more this time around… The ongoing Middle East conflict has of course delivered a third wave of inflation to Japan's shores. How might things play out this time around? records.text: 6 Global Economic Viewpoint | 21 May 2026 (let’s say, in 10 years). So given what we know today, productivity gains at the aggregate level are likely to be very small. AI is different: breadth and the productivity of innovation AI differs from past technologies because it can reach a far broader share of tasks, and the portion that is economically automatable is likely to rise quickly as models advance. New estimates already suggest potential productivity effects up to 10x larger than earlier calculations, with even small shifts in task coverage or cost‑effectiveness producing disproportionately large TFP gains. More importantly, AI can also raise the productivity of innovation itself, amplifying idea generation and turning a one‑off level boost into faster ongoing productivity growth. Even modest improvements in innovation rates can shift economies onto permanently higher trajectories, with large cumulative effects over time. AI is different (1): broader AI is different, if we are to compare it to previous innovations such as electricity or ICT. What makes AI different is that it can have an impact across a broader part of the economy. And, while today only 20% of tasks can be transformed by AI and only 23% of those tasks are cost-effective to automate, those numbers could change rapidly given how quickly AI innovation is advancing. The government has also set up a specific policy tool to support developments in the housing sector. By establishing the España crece (Spain Grows) fund, the government plans to mobilise EUR 60bn through the Official Credit Institute (ICO) to reach a total investment of around EUR 120 billion (9% of GDP), combining public and private capital. Endowed with a capital injection of EUR10.5bn from the European Recovery Plan, the fund explicitly targets private leverage to augment investment in residential developments. The fund was also part of a broader strategy of the Spanish government to extend the impact of the European Recovery Fund beyond the end of the programme in 2026. The Recovery Fund has been a key factor supporting investment growth and comes to an end this year. Since a large share of investment projects will only be completed in the first half of next year and with the España crece fund in place, we estimate that the support of the European Recovery Fund will extend beyond the end of 2026, suggesting a moderation rather than collapse of fiscal support for investment, and reducing the risk of an abrupt halt in capex momentum (Exhibit 8). The bill has the support of the White House and aims to address housing affordability. The main point of debate with the Senate was around forced sales of build-to-rent homes, which the House version removed. That is positive for housing supply as forced sales would have likely slowed the pace of build-to-rent developments. The bill, if passed by the Senate, is unlikely to have a material impact on affordability ahead of this year’s midterms. This is because the supply-side provisions in the bill are unlikely to lead to materially more construction in the near-term. • Reconciliation: Republicans are aiming to pass a party-line reconciliation bill this week to meet Trump's June 1 deadline (ahead of recess next week). records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 22 May 2026 Citi Research 3 Expansion in JGBs for individual investors could dampen bank demand The MoF is considering expanding JGBs for individual investors (Reuters, May 20). There has for some time been a focus on which investor category would increase holdings of JGBs as the BoJ normalizes its balance sheet. Some have expected demand from life insurers to grow in the super-long sector as interest rates rise, but there are now indications that duration demand is saturated. Banks have also adopted a cautious stance, and their buying has not been sufficient to stop the rise in interest rates. In this environment overseas investors have increased their holdings, and we think this has caused JGBs to cheapen until they satisfy foreign investor investment yardsticks while strengthening the linkage to overseas markets. One proposal to broaden the investment base is to expand JGBs for individual investors, but as of FY3/27 this has consisted only of widening the target market to include condominium associations. We think changes in product design would likely be next. Currently there are three types of bonds for individual investors: fixed-rate three- year, fixed-rate five-year, and variable-rate ten-year. The fixed interest rates are the benchmark rate minus 3bp for the three-year and minus 5bp for the five-year, so they are close to market rates. The Fed would have the opportunity to observe what reserve demand looks like at lower levels before it decides to consider more drastic changes in balance sheet policy as well. The large swings in the TGA over the coming quarter should give the Fed a fresh view at those levels, and what that does to money market conditions. Moreover, the Fed might want concrete evidence that banks' demand for reserves has indeed shifted lower, and the responses to the SFOS suggest that demand should remain the same over the next year, but might adjust lower should liquidity regulation changes come to fruition. This is the context for what Perli had in mind under a scenario that might lead the Fed to restart QT , and even proposed changes for liquidity rules are likely not in store until late this year or early next. We think that makes QT unlikely for this year, but with the Fed reminding markets that QT is an option, should funding pressures remain stubbornly soft, we would not rule out the Fed taking more aggressive action down the road. Moreover, limited use of the SRP amid soft conditions could lead to a degree of atrophy in participation once pressures resume, an undesirable outcome after the strides the Fed made in encouraging its use (see here). "1 Regardless of how the politics play out, we think oil markets are priced for the best case scenario and see risks to our $100/b forecast for Brent in 2026 skewed higher. Inventories continue to decline at a fast pace. Our global total oil inventory indicator, excluding the Middle East Gulf region to filter out the noise from the backlog of floating storage there, suggests the inventory builds in 2025 have already been more than offset (Figure 1). Adjusted for pre-pandemic seasonality (2017-19 seasonal average), the indicator stood at -60 mb last week, compared with -50 at the end of 2024 (Figure 2). However, the fundamental picture is significantly tighter, for several reasons. First, inventories are a lagged indicator for the effect of the ongoing supply disruption. Even if the Strait of Hormuz were to fully reopen today, it would take at least four weeks before the shipments from the Gulf start showing up materially in destination countries. In the past four weeks, this indicator suggests inventories have dropped by 150 mb. At this pace, the starting point for inventories even in the most optimistic scenario will be roughly 20 mb below the tightest level in recent history. records.text: m here the outcome will arguably depend on the resolve of the governor and his two deputies. We stick to our June call for the next hike, assuming moves toward the alleviation of Middle East tensions can be confirmed by then. While much ultimately depends on these developments, we view the latest decision as part of the groundwork for early rate hikes. Moreover, if the Middle East situation stabilizes, uncertainty over the outlook for economic activity should diminish, likely prompting the BoJ to become even more conscious of upside inflation risks. In recent years, firms have become more accustomed to passing higher costs through to prices, and the BoJ appears increasingly wary that the mechanism through which higher oil prices feed into inflation has strengthened versus the past. As a result, after a June hike, we think the BoJ will be willing to accept somewhat shorter intervals between hikes, and will make additional moves in October and April 2027 in line with our projections prior to the conflict. Our terminal rate forecast remains 1.5%. PM Takaichi’s moves are also worth watching. At this stage, measures to combat inflation, including JPY weakness, are an urgent priority for Takaichi, and given that US Treasury Secretary Bessent has also indicated the need for rate hikes, we believe she would likely continue tolerating gradual rises, though perhaps reluctantly. 22 May 2026 3 Barclays | Market Strategy Japan: Supplementary budget and hawkish BoJ

Narrow path to fiscal consolidation: Fiscal policy remains a key investor concern as estimated headroom has narrowed to ~£12bn (down by £11bn since OBR’s Spring Forecast in March), pressured by weaker growth and higher rates. Elevated spending needs and limited room to adjust fiscal rules (given Gilt market sensitivity) leave tax increases as the main lever. Fast forward to May 2026 and the combo of slower GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth and higher inflation is apparent. What may be less obvious is a sharply wider current account (CA) deficit forthcoming. Pre-war, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas anticipated an improvement in the CA deficit in 2026E to US$13bn (or 3% of GDP), from US$16bn in 2025. However, with oil seen to average US$92.5/bbl in FY26E (from US$65/bbl pre-war), we believe this would widen the trade deficit, and subsequently, the CA deficit. We forecast a CA deficit in 2026E of US$21bn, or 4.1% of GDP. At the same time, lower earners also expect worse growth prospects, but higher nominal spending, together suggesting stagflationary concerns in the economy (Exhibit 5, right). While an increase in spending most likely relates to “forced” spending on more expensive necessities, liquidity constraints are likely to cause a contraction in discretionary spending, leading to a disproportionate effect on aggregate demand compared with a similar shift in the expectations of high-income quintiles. As for the ECB, the heterogeneity of inflation and growth expectations across geographies and income levels has important implications for monetary policy transmission, making its effect less predictable and potentially weaker at the aggregate level. Taken together, the recent inflation expectations data point to a material rise in short-term expectations—with concerns around further upside risks—consistent with significant direct and indirect inflation effects from the energy shock. But longer-term expectations remain anchored, pointing to limited second-round inflation effects at this point. We expect two 25bp hikes, one in June and one in July, as the most probable timing. Signs of demand weakness and limited passthrough will likely limit stop the hiking in 2H26, in our view, but upcoming fiscal spending and private investment will probably make subsequent rate cuts unlikely. Inflation heading above 3%, but falling back close to 2% in 2028 – We nudged our inflation forecasts slightly higher again, with headline HICP now averaging 3.0% in 2026 and returning to 2.0% on average only in 2028. We see second- round effects into core inflation as far less likely than in 2022. Fiscal policy may step in again. We think interventions will primarily focus on lowering taxes on transport fuels, but measures on utility bills or income support might follow, with the fiscal cost likely a non-linear function of the price shock’s intensity. We assume mitigation costs worth about 0.5% of GDP for now. Long-end rates reached their highest level since the GFC, with likely a mix of factors contributing to the move, but no clear trigger for such a spike. A combination of hot inflation data in the US, coupled with a lack of clarity around a deal with Iran, keep fueling inflation concerns, while the data keep painting a resilient US economy both for consumer spending and the labor market. In this context, the market is becoming more concerned about the Fed’s potential inability to deliver rate cuts. But that can’t be all there is to it. An inflation-driven selloff should have led to a flatter curve or higher breakevens. Instead, we have a steeper curve and a move driven by real rates. The energy shock is still in the air, and has led to a large repricing of global monetary policy since February. However, the latest string of disappointment is coming from the domestic economy. records.text: This is also visible in the composition of loan supply. Dividend recapitalization issuance has become more difficult to execute in the USD market, as loan-to-value ratios have moved higher. As a result, dividend recapitalization deals have fallen to 12% of gross USD loan issuance year-to-date, from 21% previously. That said, they still account for roughly 20% of gross EUR loan issuance (Exhibit 15). Additionally, we believe AI-related financing spells a potential green shoot for the USD loan market. With only one compute deal so far this year, the loan market has been far less active in the AI financing wave relative to other credit markets. That said, there are a few reasons why the BSL market could be attractive for issuers. First, the lack of supply itself should support absorption as issuers continue to diversify their funding mix across markets. Second, the relatively front-loaded risk profile of many secured AI-related financings fits reasonably well with the weaker call protection and refinancing flexibility that the loan market typically offers. Third, the existence of AI-related financing in the direct lending market provides the template for either BSL takeouts of direct lending deals, or similar new issue loan deals. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 28 Saudi Arabia The kingdom’s 1Q budget outturn has drawn considerable attention, as market participants look for early evidence of the conflict’s fiscal impact. Our analysis suggests that the fiscal accounts had likely begun to drift from the FY26 plan before the conflict, which has further compounded the slippage. The 1Q’26 deficit of SAR125.7bn absorbed roughly three-quarters of the full-year envelope (SAR165bn) in a single quarter, driven mainly by spending against broadly flat revenues. Looking ahead, we expect the conflict and the Hormuz closure to reshape the picture in three respects. First, pipeline-constrained export volumes are likely to limit the revenue benefit from sharply higher oil prices. Second, defense, infrastructure repair and subsidy outlays should generate additional spending pressures from 2Q’26. Third, the FY26 budget framework, formulated under pre-war assumptions, will likely require recalibration as the new environment takes shape. Our base case envisages a budget deficit of 5.7% of GDP this year, broadly unchanged from 2025 (5.8%), with wide confidence intervals reflecting the uncertain geopolitical backdrop. records.text: te a reduction of -80bp of euro area energy HICP from the German tax cut: Since 1-May, there is a two-month reduction of the energy tax levied on fuels in Germany. Together with a lower VAT payment due to a smaller taxable base, this policy was expected to reduce German fuel prices by up to 17ct/l (7-8%). To estimate the actual impact (i.e., taking into account price changes due to moves in oil prices as well as an imperfect pass-through of the tax reduction to final consumer prices), we assume that absent the policy change, German prices would have evolved in line with French pump prices (a similar approach is applied by ifo's tracker). Changes in weekly pump prices for the two countries are shown in Exhibit 7 . The relative difference in the changes suggests that the policy measure has lowered German super fuels by -16/ct and -15/ct for diesel (around 95% of the potential ex ante pass-through). This implies a weighted change of -7.3%M for German HICP fuel prices, which is equivalent to -80bp of euro area energy inflation (-2.9%M for German HICP energy).

records.text: World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 7 JP rates: Fiscal policy back in focus Tomonobu Yamashita BofAS Japan Key theme: JGB selling fueled by supply–demand imbalance and budget risks Yen rates have surged, with the 10 ‑year JGB yield rising above 2.7% and the 30 ‑year reaching a record high. While net JGB supply is widely expected to increase in 2026 versus 2025 (see Liquid Insight: Global government bond supply update: same same, but different 14 May 2026), the May auction schedule and supplementary budget headlines are fueling selling pressure. Since late April to early May was Japan ’s national holiday period, the JGB auction schedule has been particularly crowded from mid ‑May through early June. Meanwhile, demand for JGBs has been subdued, except from Japanese pension funds. As a result, each auction is adding to selling pressure on JGBs . In addition, media reports suggest the Japanese government is considering a first supplementary budget for FY2026 to finance energy subsidies for households. Even if the Takaichi administration decides to compile the supplementary budget by the end of the current Diet session, which runs through July 17, we do not expect a near ‑term increase in auction sizes. However, this could act as an obstacle to buying JGBs on dips (see Japan Viewpoint: Cost of energy subsidies: rising risk of a supplementary budget ahead of summer 23 April 2026 ). records.text: Corporate earnings summary and company guidance Top-line growth broadly intact, but widespread margin compression Top-line growth remained broadly intact across most companies, but margin pressure has been a consistent theme. Toyota’s (TOYOTA) FY2026 results illustrate this trend clearly, with revenue rising 5.5% y/y to JPY50.7trn, while operating income declined 21.5% y/y and operating margin compressed to 7.4% from 10.0% in the prior year. The margin erosion was primarily driven by tariff impacts (JPY1.38trn) and higher input and investment costs, partially offset by improved volume and product mix as well as ongoing cost reduction efforts. Honda (HNDA) similarly reported only modest top-line expansion, with sales revenue up marginally by 0.5% y/y to JPY21.8bn, but the company saw an operating loss of JPY414.3bn, largely attributable to EV- related losses. Nissan’s (NSANY) FY2025 results were weaker, with revenue declining 4.9% y/y to JPY12.0trn, while operating profit fell to JPY58bn (from JPY69.8bn in FY2024) and operating margins narrowed to 0.5%, highlighting continued structural challenges. In contrast, the telecom sector demonstrated more stable earnings profiles, albeit with slight margin compression. NTT (NTT) reported FY2025 revenue growth of 5.1% y/y to JPY14.4trn, with EBITDA and operating profit increasing 5.7% and 3.4% y/y, respectively, although both gross and EBITDA margins declined marginally to 50.0% and 24.7%.
