records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 24 South Korea & Indonesia South Korea Given the rising likelihood of meaningfully larger fiscal spending for 2H26 and 2027, we recently raised our 2026–2027 GDP growth forecast to 3% and 2.8% (previously 2.9% and 2.4%), respectively. Semiconductor-led corporate tax revenue could provide extra fiscal revenue. In our view, the government could raise fiscal spending by W20trn for 2H26 and W90trn for 2027, likely generating upside risks to economic growth. The government is likely to prioritize investment in AI and innovation to improve potential economic growth. It may also increase welfare spending to address the K-shaped growth challenges. We recently revised up our view of the BoK rate hiking cycle to 25bps each in July 2026, October 2026, January 2027, and April 2027 towards a 3.5% terminal rate (previously 25bps each in July 2026 and October 2026, towards a 3% terminal rate). This is due to three factors: 1) the active role of fiscal policy in strengthening economic growth; 2) the risk of higher-for-longer core inflation for 2H26–1H27; and 3) historically accommodative financial conditions including for the housing market and the equity market. We may see a mix of expansionary fiscal policy and tightening monetary policy in 2H26–2027. records.text: World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 63 Gold: central banks still add gold Michael Widmer MLI (UK) Themes: inflation weighs on gold prices We lowered our 2Q26 gold price forecast to $4,500/oz in February, acknowledging market concerns over the implications of a Warsh Fed. The Iran war added additional headwinds to the yellow metal. Indeed, a stronger USD removed an incentive to increase exposure to the yellow metal. Beyond that, investors have also oscillated on what rising energy prices may mean: on days when growth concerns dominated, gold rallied; yet, when markets priced in higher inflation and a more restrictive monetary policy path, the yellow metal came under pressure. With no imminent end to the Iran war in sight, the latter dynamic has increasingly dominated activity, keeping a firm lid on gold. Linked to that, we also acknowledge the call by our colleagues in the US economics team that the Fed will not cut rates this year. Forecasts: near-term gold air pocket Gold has hit an air pocket . Still we continue to see resilient sectors. Indeed, even as Central Bank of Türkiye has reduced its gold holdings through a combination of swaps and outright sales, monetary authorities in aggregate have remained net buyers in 1Q26. In our view, this highlights gold ’s continued appeal in diversifying reserves as concerns over unorthodox US economic policies and a weaponisation of USD prevail. Household employment declined by 226k, marking the fourth consecutive drop and creating a divergence from the Establishment survey’s NFP (Nonfarm Payroll) print. This divergence is not uncommon, and we typically place more weight on the Establishment survey signal, given the survey's lower standard error (~120k vs ~500k). But the Household survey signal is still worth monitoring (Exhibit 4). Also, broader slack measures showed some weakness: U6 rose to 8.2% (highest since 2021), part-time workers for economic reasons saw an increase and unemployment duration rose as well. Labor force participation edged down to 61.8%, driven by the 55+ cohort, while prime-age participation held steady, an important offset. Overall, we see the labor market as solid, but not necessarily heating up. Wages: steady, not inflationary When judging whether the labor market is becoming hot and potentially inflationary, wage dynamics are key. One metric we track closely is the wage premium for job switchers. Measures of this premium, including from our Bank of America Institute, do not suggest the labor market has tightened to start the year. Atlanta Fed data show some modest firming after the premium effectively disappeared between mid-2024 and mid-2025. records.chunk_id: Has the Fed lost its inflation anchor, again?.pdf-1-1
records.text: differ across economic agents. In 2022, concern first surged in market-based expectations and economists’ forecasts; consumers’ doubts emerged later but have proved persistent (Figure 2). This is clearest in the volatility and dispersion of consumer inflation expectations, which Ricardo Reis has highlighted as one of the few late-1960s signs that the inflation anchor was loosening. In 2026, this may also reflect political distortions in consumer sentiment surveys, but it remains troubling. Notably, the volatility and dispersion of economists’ forecasts are also beginning to rise, while in market-based measures, the sensitivity of 5-yr expectations to moves in 1-yr expectations is increasing. None of this is alarming on its own. But with consumers’ view of the anchor still not recovered from 2022, further pressure from economists’ forecasts and market-based measures will warrant attention. Especially so in response to incoming inflation data and, more importantly, the Fed’s reaction in the months ahead. For now, the Fed hasn’t lost its inflation anchor, but the pressure still requires care. records.text: US Rates Weekly 22 May 2026 Citi Research 7 We still see “fair value” of 5y swap spreads wider from here We entered 2026 bullish on swap spreads, favoring the 5y sector, and our conviction remains even after the recent rebound from the March lows (see Short- End Notes: 2026 Money Markets Outlook). We have had a few discussions with clients who think the move in 5y spreads may be running out of steam at this juncture. In our view, there remains significant scope for 5y spreads to move towards -20bp to -22bp by YE26. As a reminder, the Fed first needs to reduce the demand for bank reserves to materially bring down the size of the balance sheet relative to Q4 of last year. We estimate that a reduction of almost $500bn in reserve demand is achievable, although it will take some work on the regulatory/supervisory side (see US Rates Weekly - May refunding preview – Will auction sizes ever be increased?). We view a reduction in demand for reserves as akin to increasing supply and thus we think this should be exceptionally beneficial to spreads, assuming it can be achieved in the next one or two years. (See Alejandra’s section for more details.) How do we translate that into a price for 5y spreads? First, we can look at 1y1y SOFR/FF as a rough proxy for how the market thinks about the Fed balance sheet, and from there see where 5y spreads could trade (Figure 12). records.text: 58 World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 Uruguay: Coping with the oil shock Sebastian Rondeau BofAS The government is cushioning the oil shock. It announced a fuel price hike of only 7% for April, but more hikes should come. Uruguay is affected by the shock as it imports 100% of the oil. Inflation increased to 3.1% yoy from 2.9% yoy in March (vs 3.7% in 2025 and 5.5% in 2024), close to the bottom of the target band (3 -6%). Inflation should return to the center of the target as BCU eased policy to avoid further disinflation and appreciation. We forecast inflation at 3.9% in 2026 and 4.5% in 2027. 12 -month ahead inflation forecasts increased to 4.8% (BCRA survey), from a 4.5% low. BCU kept rates on hold at 5.75%, after cutting 75bp in March, 100bp cut in January and a 50bp cut in December (from a 9.25% peak in April). This is amid fast inflation progress and slow growth. BCU considered a rate around 7.5% was neutral territory. We fo recast BCU to raise the policy rate next year to 7% as shocks dissipate. In January the government announced it would intervene in the FX (most likely buying USD forward) to avoid a further appreciation of the UYU. Activity soft patch GDP growth slowed down to 1,8% last year, amid Argentina ’s headwinds, vs the 3.5% GDP rebound in 2024 (following weather normalization). GDP was flat in 4Q (+0.1 qoqsa). We forecast a 1.5% expansion this year, downside risks, amid expected fiscal consolidation and oil shock. Argentina could become a tailwind eve ntually.

records.text: CDS Relative Value Systematic single-name screens – update With four weeks having passed, we update our systematic cheap and rich screens and take a look at the performance of the screens identified in our previous update. Top cheap and rich names We screen for cheap and rich names based on an algorithmic approach. For details on the methodological framework, please refer to Systematic single-name screens – review, 8 February 2019. Our screen for cheap names consists of a ranking based on 50% of the "spread momentum" metric (using a 375-day look-back period). It also uses 50% of the "stock price moving average" metric (using 20- and 100-day look-back periods). The first metric picks names where the current spread is above the average spread when normalising for realised volatility, while the second metric picks names that have seen improvement in their equity price. Our screen for rich names consists of a ranking based on 20% of the "spread momentum" metric (using a 375-day look-back period). It also uses 80% of the "stock price moving average" metric (using 20- and 100-day look-back periods). The first metric picks names where the current spread is below the average spread when normalising for realised volatility, while the second metric picks names that have not seen improvement in their equity price. To ensure tradability, the screens are restricted to names with an average weekly trading volume exceeding $50mn, as per the most recent six-month DTCC report. 22 May 2026 32

records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 13 Select Economy Discussion North America United States Resilient activity, stable labor market data, but sticky core inflation with upside risks from higher energy prices have shifted market pricing towards a greater chance of rate hikes than cuts this year. We continue to think the chance of cuts is much greater than hikes and think core inflation annualized closer to 2% in summer data will allow Fed officials to cut rates if/when the labor market weakens further. Our base case includes rate cuts in September, October, and December this year to a 2.75-3% policy rate. GDP rose 2.0% in Q1, due partly to a rebound in government activity following the Q4 government shutdown. Real consumption growth has been slower in recent quarters but remains resilient. We continue to expect solid growth in 2026, due partly to continued strength in AI- related business investment. The rise in energy prices, if sustained for many months, could weigh on GDP by a few tenths of a percentage point this year. Core PCE inflation has been sticky above 3%YoY while core CPI has slowed below 3%, an abnormal divergence as CPI typically runs stronger than PCE. Headline inflation will continue to be strong in the near term as energy prices have remained elevated. records.text: he Bank Research Beyond the structurally induced expansion of the federal budgetary deficit (mainly encompassing defense and investments), the sustained economic weakness is anticipated to adversely affect Germany's public finances. In this context, it should be noted that we project only 0.5% growth this year, implying that the economy's (negative) output gap and, consequently, the cyclically-induced government deficit should remain at a similar high level as last year (see Figure 10). All in all, we anticipate the general government deficit (national accounting) could reach about 4.1% of GDP in 2026 (2025: 2.7% of GDP) (see Figure 10 and 11). While our forecast sits slightly below the government's current projection of 4.25% of GDP (see also the May 2026 projections by the German Stability Council), it is a little higher than the Deutsche Bundesbank's estimate of around 4% of GDP (see Monthly Report for May 2026). While we expect the ONS seasonal adjustment process to capture this eventually, for now it means that we also assume a weaker profile throughout the year with Q4 2026 growth at just 0.1% QQ to capture this trend. Questions remain over the path for inflation. The challenges around the inflation forecast remain as they were at the time of the last GEOS: Hormuz; fiscal intervention on energy bills; degree of pass-through into second-round effects. Each of these remains an unknown and, in their absence, we’ve left the forecast largely unchanged. That is to say we continue to expect a surge in non-core inflation with only limited second-round effects in services. We continue to watch two themes as we monitor the forecast. The first is whether or not the government opts to intervene on energy bills. Doing so would mechanically lower Q3 inflation but, absent the demand destruction that higher prices would otherwise bring, risks a strong profile through 2027. The second is Hormuz, where the absence of a resolution presents predominantly upside risks as we approach summer. Our economists highlight that South Korea’s economic performance is heavily skewed towards semiconductor exports—a sector that represents a relatively small segment of the labor market. Given that growth is not broad-based, we do not expect the BoK to implement a series of aggressive hikes. Meanwhile, Indian inflation has surprised to the downside in the past month, due to lower food prices, which gives the RBI room to wait, in our view. Also, we do not think the RBI will respond to currency weakness with multiple rate hikes. records.text: When the balance sheet is roughly stable, swings in the TGA account for the bulk of week-to-week reserve volatility; over the last six months, the standard deviation of weekly reserve changes would have been about 70% lower had the TGA been stable or steps taken to sterilize TGA changes (Exhibit 15). The TGA ’s relative volatility versus the Fed’s other non-reserve liabilities has been true over the longer run as well (Exhibit 16). A buffer to mitigate against a 95th percentile one month drop in reserves due to the TGA requires about $200bn today. Rather than maintaining that buffer as a regular course of business, the Fed could consider using short-term repo operations to supplement the SRP in smoothing through temporary TGA jumps around events like tax payment dates. Running a smaller reserve buffer on a day-to-day basis could also encourage short-term rates to set modestly higher versus IORB, increasing incentives for banks to lend. A change in Treasury’s cash management policy to allow some portion of its cash balance to be lent in the repo market when short-term rates exceed IORB could also achieve a similar outcome without requiring the Fed to temporarily expand its balance sheet. This possibility was discussed at Treasury’s most recent refunding decision, but any possible change in policy seems likely to take time, with the TBAC minutes noting that more study around “operational and implementation considerations” is needed. Three related factors underpin this view. • Reduced supply chain resilience. Following a two-de- cade period in which forces promoting free trade and more efficient supply-chains produced a subdued 0.5% pace of global core goods price gains, the global backdrop has shifted. Starting with the 2018-19 trade war, a series of supply shocks have reshaped the flow of global goods trade. While the 2021-23 price surge has abated, core goods prices rose 0.9% over 2024-25 amidst sluggish goods spending. At the start of the year, we anticipated a pickup in demand to lift core goods prices by 1.5%, with upward pressure concentrated in the US. • Wage shocks unwind with tight labor markets. Despite wide divergences in business cycle outcomes during this expansion, service price inflation has remained broadly elevated. This synchronization reflects the legacy of a common global shock to labor cost inflation in the after- math of the pandemic (Figure 2). records.text: M Update 2 Our forecast for the general government deficit and growth is unchanged: We continue to forecast the 2026 fiscal balance of the general government (federal + regional + municipal + social security) in the national accounts at -3.9%-GDP, which would be a deficit expansion of 120bp vs 2025, slightly above consensus (+110bp) but a smaller step-up than the Bundesbank's December forecast (+140bp) and the government's own projection (+155bp) (see summary of forecasts here). records.text: The balance sheet baseline and illustrative scenarios In equilibrium we expect the Fed to keep reserves roughly stable as a share of bank assets, which requires asset growth to keep pace with currency demand, TGA growth, and what is needed for reserves to grow in line with the broader banking system. Assuming 4.5% trend nominal growth in both currency and bank assets, and a TGA that grows with the trend in Treasury’s weekly gross cash withdrawals, that implies about $9bn per month in expansion for currency, $11bn per month to keep pace with growth in bank assets, and $5bn per month for the purposes of TGA growth. A $25bn per month run rate is now somewhat above the recently announced $10bn per month pace of reserve management purchases (RMPs)—a marked deceleration from the initial $40bn per month pace. Given the extent of easing in funding conditions (discussed in greater detail below), we expect monthly RMPs to slow to an average of $5bn through Q1 of next year, which we estimate would take reserves to 11% of bank assets—a level we estimate would be consistent with tri-party repo rates settling slightly below IORB (Exhibit 8). Beyond that point we assume RMPs return to a trend-like pace of $25bn per month. Here, we formalize this relationship based on the Domar condition and derive the change in inflation required to absorb a deterioration in the primary balance. Let Bt denote nominal government debt outstanding at time t, Yt nominal GDP , PBt the nominal primary balance, gt the real growth rate, and πt the inflation rate. Define the debt/GDP ratio as bt, and let it denote the nominal interest rate corresponding to debt servicing costs. The government’s nominal budget constraint is given by: Bt+ 1 = (1 + it)Bt− PB t We impose the debt stability condition bt+ 1 = bt = b , meaning that the debt/GDP ratio remains constant over time. Under this condition, the following relationship for the inflation rate πt can be derived from the government budget constraint: πt = (1 + it) − PB t Bt 1 + gt − 1 Therefore, the relationship between a change in the nominal primary balance ΔPBt and the corresponding change in inflation Δπt is given by: Δ πt = − 1 1 + gt Δ PB t Bt The simulation of inflation under various PB deterioration scenarios uses this expression. The government looks likely to resume electricity and gas bill subsidies over the summer, which would probably limit an increase in core CPI to some extent. It is generally estimated that higher crude oil prices are reflected in consumer prices meaningfully with a time lag of 6-12 months. We thus think inflation may well rise towards 3% again early next year. Implications for monetary policy — Both headline and core CPI have remained under the 2% target, but as discussed above this is due largely to special factors. Therefore, we think the BoJ continues to assess that underlying inflation is coming closer to 2%. Indeed, the BoJ began announcing the CPI figure without special factors from end-March, in our view as it had expected the current situation. At the April MPM three board members called for a rate hike and voted against the status quo, a situation that had never happened under Governor Ueda’s leadership. The sense of vigilance against upside inflation risks has been increasing among monetary policymakers, and board members Kazuyuki Masu and Junko Koeda made comments apparently aiming to pave the way for next rate hikes in their recent speeches. We therefore do not think today’s result will diminish expectations for early rate hikes and continue to expect the next hike in June. records.text: Comparing hedge fund and mutual fund positioning This week we published our Hedge Fund Trend Monitor and Mutual Fundamentals reports, which analyze holdings at the start of Q2 2026. Our analyses cover 1,059 hedge funds with $4.6 trillion of gross equity positions ($3.1 trillion long, $1.5 trillion short) and 509 large-cap active mutual funds with $3.9 trillion in equity assets. US equity hedge funds have ridden the recent wave of Momentum outperformance to deliver solid YTD absolute returns while most mutual funds have struggled to keep pace with rising benchmarks. According to estimates from GS Prime Services, US equity long/short funds have returned 7% YTD, supported by beta and long alpha. Our basket of Hedge Fund popular long positions (GSTHHVIP) has returned 13% compared with 7% for the equal-weight S&P 500 and 27% for a basket of stocks with concentrated short interest. The average large-cap mutual fund has returned 7% YTD, but only 30% of funds are outperforming their benchmarks, below the historical average of 37%. Hedge funds and mutual funds each carry above-average equity market exposures. Hedge funds and mutual funds initially reduced exposure to US equities at the onset of geopolitical tensions in March but hedge funds have since lifted net leverage to the 85th percentile relative to the last five years. records.text: ort strength and FX recovery Source: Bloomberg, Macrobond, Morgan Stanley Research We see AXJ FX and rates markets being driven by two key themes in 2H26: 1) the trajectory for oil prices; and 2) the industrial super-cycle. The path for oil prices remains uncertain: Our oil strategists' base case is that oil exports via the Strait of Hormuz will resume from June, although oil prices may stay elevated at ~US$100-110/barrel through 3Q26 and ease only to US$90/barrel by year-end due to operational and logistical challenges. This has two effects on AXJ currencies: First, the reopening of the Strait should allow AXJ currencies to rally as markets price out risks of severe disruptions to Asia economic activity from energy supply shortages. Second, oil prices staying elevated implies that there could still be an impact on economies' energy trade balances and hence current account balances. In our view, currencies that: 1) are fundamentally more exposed to energy and food disruptions; 2) have underperformed recently since the start of the Middle East tensions; and 3) historically do well when US real yields and inflation breakevens decline alongside strong equities, may outperform initially.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Financial Conditions: The market is doing the Fed's work so far Following the conflict in the Middle East and the uncertainty it brings to the next steps for monetary policy, we include the evolution of our FRB/US-based model of financial conditions, which aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. The index includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate, using the Federal Reserve’s FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since hostilities in the Middle East began on February 28, the tightening in financial conditions is equivalent to about a 35bp rise in the federal funds rate. Since the April 7 ceasefire announcement, however, financial conditions have eased by 37bps. The tightening reversed all of the easing seen earlier this year, most of which occurred between the December and January FOMC meetings, and was primarily driven by a weaker U.S. dollar. CHF weakness versus USD, NOK and AUD suggests that some carry fundamentals are emerging in an environment w here market stress have corrected lower. CHF outperformance versus the other G10 currencies reflects stresses in the stagflation narrative where the counter-cyclical properties of CHF have prevailed. Our previous analysis suggests that broader CHF apprecia tion is unlikely in the absence of a renewed spike in vol of vol – a strong historic driver for CHF. This is still a tail risk for as long there are no discernible signs of a lasting ceasefire, broader CHF losses are unlikely to materialize. Rather, we would choose to be selective in our short CHF recommendations and USD/CHF higher stands out as a trade that leverages on both wider rate differentials, stronger US data relative to Switzerland and the flattening of the US yield curve which has correlated well with a stronger USD. With global central banks focused on the inflation/growth trade-off, we suspect that the urgency from the SNB to talk CHF lower has declined in similar fashion to 2023, Inflation targeting remains at the heart of policy for the SNB and we expect this to be focus at the June quarterly meeting. records.text: output accelerated to a 3.6%ar in the three months through March, tracking well above our forecast for a 2.5%ar 1H26 gain. Behind this lift is strong business spending on capital equipment, led by an ongoing tech boom. At the same time, global retail spending rebounded from a weak turn into the new year, with global sales volumes outside China rising at a 2.7%ar. Taken together, the range of potential inflation outcomes over the coming year has widened. Risks are elevated that an ener- gy price shock squeezes household purchasing power and depresses business sentiment, raising the specter of a negative growth shock raising unemployment rates. This outcome would ultimately prove to be disinflationary. At the same time, the interaction of persistent elevated oil prices and solid growth raises the risk of core inflation breaking above 3%. This outcome would likely set the stage for a new round of global monetary policy tightening. For goods prices, a return to the commons The message from the incoming reports is that pressure on core goods prices is building. Over the first four months of the year, core goods prices rose at a 1.3% rate (ex China and Türkiye), in line with our forecast at the start of the year. But model estimates, incorporating both survey measures of goods demand and pipeline cost pressures, point to gains accelerating to a 2.5-3%ar over the coming six months (Fig- ure 5). records.text: uctivity upside could be 10x the current estimates AI differs from earlier technologies in that it can take on a broader range of tasks and continuously expand what it can do. As AI models improve and the technology spreads to more tasks and becomes cheaper, macro gains could be much larger. We think AI could have a much bigger impact on aggregate productivity—up to 10x larger than what we ’re seeing today. Global growth is at 3.5% and AI-driven productivity gains are currently adding 10 basis points per year to it. But in the best case, AI-driven productivity could lift growth by about 1% a year over the next decade, increasing global growth to 4.5%. Innovation productivity is the real multiplier AI can also lift the productivity of innovation itself, speeding up idea generation and improving the growth rate, not just the level, of long‑run output. This means that even modest improvements will compound over time into substantially stronger economic outcomes. In our view, there will be significant increases in productivity in the long run, but not just immediately. Diffusion will create winners and losers Countries with stronger capacity to adopt AI, especially the US and China, will capture productivity increases earlier and more fully than potential laggards, such as Europe and EM economies. Even small differences in variables today, like diffusion, could not only drive bigger one-time productivity boosts but also leave some permanently ahead while others fall behind never

records.text: Exports and the Property Market Key to Watch With growth slowing in April but policymakers not feeling the urgency to ease policy, we think there are two parts of the economy that deserve close monitoring. First, exports have been the engine of Chinese growth over the past few years, and signs that they are coming under significant pressure would change policymakers’ thinking. As of April, other than in the Middle East, where the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has stopped shipments, we have not seen weakening in Chinese exports to EM destinations (Exhibit 10). Second, there have been some encouraging signs from the property market in top-tier cities. Both the 30-city daily transactions of new properties and the 16-city daily transactions of existing homes have been relatively stable this year. US Home Prices: Home price appreciation has slowed as demand remains challenged. Inventories of existing homes have picked up but are still low. However, the recent rise in mortgage rates means some of the improvement in affordability has reversed. Last year, the median income was 1.03 times the income needed to qualify for a loan on a median-priced home; that rose to 1.17 times in February but has since fallen back to about 1.08 times as of mid- May. Our housing strategists expect home price growth to reaccelerate later this year as rates decline, but it should remain limited at 2% this year and next. US Conference Board: Consumer confidence remains low, though it picked up slightly in March and April despite the oil shock. The labor market differential has also improved over the past two months, matching the decline in jobless claims and rebound in payrolls. WEDNESDAY, MAY 27 US Richmond & Dallas Fed: Both the Dallas Fed and Richmond Fed surveys posted solid manufacturing readings in April, supported by firm production and demand components. In line with outright spread dynamics, this points to limited evidence of a UK CDS specific skew in financials. A cross-sectional view of CDS versus cash moves since 8 May offers additional insights. We plot relative moves in both CDS and cash to abstract from broader market dynamics. For non- financials ( Figure 7), while performance appears scattered, a notable share of names exhibit wrong-way moves, highlighting a disconnect between the two markets. In particular, focusing on UK names, we see the largest cluster sits in the bottom-right quadrant, where CDS has widened while cash has tightened, suggesting the broader underperformance of UK CDS versus cash in non-financials has continued to build in several names more recently. Within financials ( Figure 8), we again see some presence of wrong‑way moves, but no UK names sit in the bottom-right quadrant. Instead, for UK names, CDS widening has been accompanied by a corresponding widening in cash spreads. That said, the UK financial names that have tightened in CDS have seen their cash bonds widen, reflecting a dislocation in the opposite direction to what we highlighted in non‑financials. 22 May 2026 28 Barclays | European Credit Alpha: Higher rates require stable growth

China’s aluminium market has been oversupplied in recent weeks, with inventories building. Similarly, prices on the country ’s physical market have been underperforming those on the Shanghai Futures Exchange, reinforcing the absence of aluminium shortages domestically. Hence, there is apprehension that more aluminium units could be shipped abroad, but China has actually increased net imports of primary aluminium YTD. Incidentally, the government also imposes a 15% export duty, making refined exports not very economic at current prices. The Big Picture Sifting through the detailed April activity data, we draw three conclusions about the current state of the Chinese economy. First, despite the sizeable disappointment in the official data release, the picture of a bifurcated economy has not changed (Exhibit 8). Second, the ongoing Middle East conflict and higher energy prices have negatively impacted the Chinese economy. This includes lower production of chemicals and processed petroleum products, squeezed margins for downstream businesses, and higher inflation and lower real income for households. We continue to expect sequential real GDP growth to slow from 5.3% qoq annualized in Q1 to 4.0% in Q2 (Exhibit 9). Third, the Chinese economy has so far been more flexible than expected in adapting to higher oil prices. Consumers bought EVs rather than ICE cars. records.text: 8 Europe Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 is taking comfort from tightening in financial conditions which they say can give them time to assess whether to hike or not. Why do we still expect modest hikes? We still think the BoE is likely to hike twice (with risks of one) in coming months to guard against second round effects. We expect energy prices to remain high through the year (with oil close to $100) and we think this elevated shock can raise risks of second round effects, especially given above-target inflation in the past few years, consumer sensitivity to high inflation and already elevated inflation/wage expectations. Inflation is likely to pick up in coming months, and survey indicators point to elevated input/output prices, increasing risks of companies passing on costs to consumers. We would be cautious in overinterpreting the downside surprise in April services inflation/ big fall in April payrolls, given erratic components driving some of the fall. Payrolls tend to be revised often and in April revisions are normally large. Other survey indicators of labour market are showing some signs of stabilization. Moreover, the BoE is currently taking some comfort from the tightening in financial conditions weighing on inflation, but the BoE actually needs to credibly deliver on the hikes priced in to maintain those tight financial conditions. There are a few risks to our call. June can’t be fully ruled out, especially if the DMP shows another leg up in inflation expectation

records.text: M Asia Pacific Insight 8 Views by Market China We see USD/CNH heading lower towards ~6.70 in 2H26 as USD weakens and China's trade balance remains strong with exports supported by the industrial cycle. The RMB gains may be moderate though as exporters' FX conversion ratios are already at the top end of the range in recent years, the CFETS basket is at elevated levels and is positively correlated with USD, which we expect to weaken, and the PBOC is unlikely to deploy currency appreciation to address structural growth imbalances given still-soft domestic demand. We see China rates outperforming its peers by staying largely range-bound. Upside pressure on yields may be constrained by still-soft domestic demand, keeping China's inflation pressures relatively lower ( Exhibit 10 ) and suggesting limited prospects of rate hikes. There is also a lack of impulse from policy, as our economists do not expect further monetary or fiscal easing for the rest of the year. records.text: M Asia Pacific Insight 6 At the same time, the industrial cycle should help to support growth, particularly in export-oriented economies like Korea and Taiwan. Korea and Singapore screen as economies which see more growth support from the industrial cycle and higher inflation pressures, suggesting that there could be more scope for monetary policy tightening expectations to build in these markets. Our economists see most central banks in the region delivering rate hikes over 2026- 27, with most scope for hikes in the Philippines, Korea, India, and Indonesia (Exhibit 11 ). The exceptions to this hiking trend are China and Thailand. Historically, yields peak only after the hiking starts: Markets are already pricing in more rate hikes than our economists anticipate and have room to come down should the Strait of Hormuz re-open. Historical experience suggests that yields typically peak only after the start of the hiking cycle (Exhibit 12 ). records.text: US Rates Weekly 22 May 2026 Citi Research 5 On term premium, we entered 2026 skeptical that there would be a large compression, mostly because bond yields had moved so high globally (see US Rates Weekly - 2026 Outlook – Battle for Accommodation). For some background, term premium has been roughly unchanged since the move higher during the tariff shock last April (Figure 7). Here, our definition of ‘term premium’ is the residual between the 2s10s curve and 2y yields using a sample starting from 1995 (we also include the Fed’s ACM model). For example, the term premium compression from 2010 to 2020 could be somewhat attributed to the decline in Bund yields and the depreciation of the EUR, which likely led to increased USD investment (Figure 8). This likely pushed investment into the US to pursue positive yields. With continued upward pressure on yields globally, we struggle to make the case for a large term premium compression. This is why we continue to favor the 5y point as our favorite for longs and see continued steepening risks. It is challenging to find a catalyst for higher term premium, given that global yields have remained high for some time now. Risks could appear later this year or next year as the US Treasury will eventually increase coupon auction sizes, which we forecast for 2027, and the US government will likely hit the debt ceiling, raising downgrade risk in 2027. records.text: h the former this time, but if it opts for the latter, the budget could swell to several trillion yen. For example, Democratic Party for the People (DPP) leader Tamaki has argued for a supplementary budget of around JPY3trn that would add support for SME financing and measures to address supply-chain bottlenecks to gasoline and electricity/gas subsidies 6 . A proposal for a budget of that size has also reportedly surfaced within the government (TBS, 21 May). As for timing and scale, the first supplementary budget for FY22 under the Kishida administration provides a useful reference point. In recent years, supplementary budgets have typically been compiled from autumn into winter at a scale of more than JPY10trn ( Figure 3), but the first supplementary budget for FY22 was enacted in May and amounted to JPY2.7trn. It was compiled primarily to fund gasoline subsidies, much like the current case, after crude oil prices surged following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February that year, and it was financed entirely through deficit-financing JGBs. The TBS report cited above (21 May) also says the package would total JPY3trn and be financed through the issuance of deficit-financing JGBs. However, because the deficit-financing JGB issuance planned for the previous fiscal year is expected to be reduced due to stronger tax revenues, the apparent intention is to keep any new issuance of such bonds within that range in order to limit the market impact. records.text: JGB transaction data: April sees a recovery in JGB investment from the previous month This section in an extract from Japan Flow Update: JGB transaction data: April sees a recovery in JGB investment from the previous month, 20 May 2026. Please refer to the original report for a detailed analysis. April saw slower buying by overseas investors amid continued tensions in the Middle East, but a recovery in investment by trusts, taking JGB investment to JPY6.3trn, back to roughly the same level as in February. By maturity, overseas investors turned to net selling in superlong bonds for the first time since December 2024, but insurers switched to net buying for the first time in nine months, while the pace of net buying by trust banks also recovered, keeping net purchases above JPY1trn for a sixth straight month. In long-term bonds, overseas investors, who had been heavy net sellers the previous month, returned to net buying of JPY1.0trn, with the total recovering to around JPY2.0trn, roughly the same level as in February. In medium-term bonds, while city banks, regional banks and agricultural and forestry-related financial institutions led net purchases, foreigner buying, which had doubled in the previous month, fell sharply, but total net purchases still increased slightly from the previous month. records.Author: Bruna Skarica
records.text: e find hard to align with the market pricing of the BoE for 2 hikes, followed by some chance of further hikes next year. We understand market participants have to place some weight on the Bank's adverse Scenario C, where commodity prices inflect higher and the Bank hikes 4 times – but the scenario embeds no recession, which seems unlikely to us. Hence, even in this scenario we would see at most 2 hikes. We also understand the nervousness around the fiscal impulse, but we find it somewhat puzzling that the market is not more focused on the degree to which the governing party is now communicating the electoral imperative of reducing "the cost of living". With borrowing constrained, any hypothetical further spending will have to come from higher taxes. The recent political pivot to inflation makes us a bit more comfortable with the assumption that we will avoid taxes that raise spot inflation, such as the employer NICs hike. To us, the biggest upside risks to our forecasts, outside of oil and gas prices, are regulatory decisions embedding the inflationary overshoot, i.e. an outsized NLW hike from April 2027. But for now, we continue to look for a BoE hold through this year, with this call underpinned by commodity price assumptions close to the Bank's Scenario B.

records.text: World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 65 Aluminum: Middle East supply headwinds Michael Widmer MLI (UK) Themes: supply headwinds bigger than hit to demand The Middle East conflict will likely impact both metals supply and demand. On the supply side, aluminium is one of the most exposed commodities, with disruptions at smelters in the Middle East, a region that accounts for just under 10% of global supply, li kely lasting up to 12 month after the conflict is settled. As such, the hit to demand is not strong enough to flip our baseline aluminium balance for now. Still, we acknowledge the downside risk to global economic activity from higher oil prices, even if markets treat the energy shock predominantly as a monetary phenomenon for now, i.e. energy prices are a bit higher but still contained. Granted, inventories in the US, Europe and China provide a temporary buffer. But the longer disruptions last, the higher the likelihood that shortages in different parts of the supply chain could hardwire a slowdown, beyond just higher feedstock prices. Forecasts: no obvious candidate to increase production Aluminium supply from the Middle East is now contracting . This one reason, we pulled forward our $4,000/t ($1.93/lb) price forecast from 2Q27 to 4Q26. Indeed, some of the output losses will take time to normalise, with EGA saying that rebuilding the 1.6 mt Al Taweelah smelter, which was destroyed by an Iranian rocket attack, could take up to one year. records.text: more substantive shifts in banks’ reserve demand. Allowing banks to include pre-pledged collateral at the Fed’s discount window and FHLB borrowing capacity in liquidity calculations—both the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and internal liquidity stress tests (ILSTS)—is one possible route. Our banks team has estimated that giving banks credit in net cash outflows—the denominator of the LCR— for these sources of liquidity could be worth up to 29pp of LCR upside across the top 7 banks (assuming 50% of the estimated pre-pledged discount window capacity were included). Whether this impact—which would boost banks’ surplus HQLA in the LCR calculation by about $600bn—would result in a one-for-one reduction in reserve demand would depend on a range of considerations, including banks’ willingness to increase day-to-day/intraday reliance on contingent sources of liquidity to settle payments. Willingness to return to pre-GFC reliance on contingent sources of liquidity—about 1.5% of bank assets—would be consistent with about $375bn in headroom to shrink the balance sheet in today’s terms. Accounting for trend growth in bank assets and non-reserve liabilities, keeping the balance sheet stable to 2Q27, or shrinking by $20bn/mo through YE26 would achieve such a shift. records.text: remium JGB yield movements continue to be driven by the term premium, and any additional inflation risk premium stemming from fiscal concerns could trigger a further sharp surge in the term premium. We have argued that macroeconomic uncertainty caused by higher crude oil prices and related factors, ie, the inflation risk premium, has been leading the rise in JPY IRS rates (see Macroeconomic uncertainty spilling into JPY IRS and volatility, 30 April), and the same is true of the JGB term premium. The recent JGB term premium has surged to well above the fair value implied by long-term drivers such as JGB supply-demand conditions. This upside deviation from the long-term fair value can be explained by short-term factors such as the rise in the inflation risk premium since last autumn. Figure 13shows a decomposition of the fair value of the 10y JGB term premium into long-term factors and short-term factors, ie the inflation risk premium component, measured by the change in 10y BEI since October 2025 6 . Looking ahead, with the outlook for the Middle East situation still highly uncertain, factors related to higher crude oil prices, as seen in the sharp acceleration in the April PPI announced on 15 May, are likely to continue pushing up the inflation risk premium. records.text: 4 US Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 Special factors When thinking about the labor market outlook for 2026 and 2027, it is important to take into account a few factors: the upcoming World Cup, summer weakness in jobs, the supply shock from tighter immigration policies and its impact on breakven job growth, and risks of QCEW-driven payroll revisions. i) World Cup effect: temporary, modest boost The 2026 FIFA World Cup (June-July) is likely to provide a temporary lift to payrolls, particularly in leisure & hospitality, trade & transportation, construction and professional & business services. Some headline estimates suggest ~185k jobs could be added. However, several factors will likely limit the measured immediate impact on payrolls: i) a significant portion of demand will likely be met via overtime (which does not increase payrolls), rather than temporary hiring, ii) independent contractor usage (e.g., security, logistics) is not captured in the Establishment survey, and iii) regular visitors are expected to avoid host cities (tourism substitution), and this would offset some of the boost from the World Cup. Looking at Copa America 2024, roughly one-quarter the scale of the World Cup in terms of attendance, we saw no discernible impact on national payrolls. Hence, we pencil in only a modest temporary bump, which is expected to play out as follows: i) June: about a 40k bump in payrolls, primarily via temporary leisure & hospitality hiring, ii) July: no impact from the World Cup

records.text: US Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 5 Fed: labor solid enough to stay put, not hot enough to hike The April FOMC minutes are broadly consistent with our labor market outlook. Participants noted that labor market conditions are expected to remain broadly stable, with risks to employment still tilted to the downside. Admittedly, this meeting took place before the April jobs report. But in our view, the bottom line is that the FOMC is not yet ready to give the labor market an “all clear,” despite the recent improvement in the data. In turn, rate hikes are probably still a ways away. For the Fed to hike under Warsh, we think core PCE inflation would have to take another leg up (to around 3.5% or higher), and the u-rate would have to fall to 4.0% or lower. The Fed might hike sooner if wages were to accelerate or long-term inflation expectations were to unanchor, but there is no sign of that for now. The true test lies ahead Finally, while both the labor market and consumer spending have held up in the last couple of months since the start of the Iran war, the real test lies ahead. Tax refund- related tailwinds have supported consumption in recent months, even in the face of higher gas prices, particularly for higher-income households. Our base case remains that consumption growth will stay near trend. records.text: Largest downside surprise since May 2023: With retail sales increasing only n 0.2% yoy and fixed asset investment contracting 8% yoy in April, our China MAP score (measuring data surprise relative to consensus forecast) turned the most negative since China reopening from the Covid pandemic. Looking through the details of the data, however, we do not think the economy has weakened as much as the latest batch of official data suggests. The impact of the Iran war is showing: Industrial production missed consensus n expectations by around 2pp in April. Chemicals and processed petroleum products showed the largest sequential declines in physical output, pointing to the negative impact of the energy-supply shock. We estimate that these sectors can explain around half of the data miss in industrial production, while the other half may be related to residual seasonality that should reverse in the next two months. Retail sales distorted by government policies: The government-subsidized n consumer goods trade-in program boosted auto and home appliance sales by pulling forward replacement demand for consumer durables. We are seeing a payback effect now. In addition, the increase in the auto purchase tax at the beginning of 2026 has further weighed on auto sales. Although these factors will continue to pressure retail sales for the remainder of this year, they should not be interpreted as a sharp deterioration in the household consumption trend. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. Volume data from July 2020 onwards represents the combined total traded volume across EBS and Reuters sources. Prior to July 2020, we aggregate total traded volume from EBS with estimated trading volume from Reuters, which is calculated as a product of total paid-given count and average trade size. To estimate average trade size prior to July 2020 we use all future data for total trading volume and trade count. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 29 Brazil & Mexico Brazil Petrobras has been sustaining domestic fuel prices systematically below the international parity (70-80%). Given this, the administration recently announced subsidies for gasoline and diesel, opening room for Petrobras to hike prices without impacting consumers at the same extent. In the meantime, CPI inflation continues running at higher-than-target level, including in the April reading, contributing to further de-anchor medium- and long-term expectations. We increase our CPI inflation forecast for 2026YE to 3.9% YoY. Accordingly, we now expect Copom to interrupt the cutting cycle at 13.75% in Sep-26 (from 13.25% in Dec-26); their recently adopted more hawkish stance supports this view. We continue expecting them to resume the interest rate cuts in 2H27, ending the year at 11.75% (from 11.25%). records.text: ta represents the average daily market spread based on quotes taken every 30 seconds in the order book aggregated across EBS and Reuters on a volume weighted basis. The spread signal is calculated as the ratio of the current spread relative to the prior one-year median spread. The values are then smoothed using a 20-day moving average. For example, a multiple of 1 indicates that the current average spread is equal to the historical median spread for that currency pair, whereas a multiple reading of 2 indicates that the current average spread for that given currency pair is twice as wide as its historical median. Turbulence is a price-based measure of the joint unusualness of G10 currency returns. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 21 May 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General H as the Fed lost its inflation anchor, again? The more ships that stay anchored in the Strait of Hormuz, the quicker oil inventories are run down and the risks of an even more destabilizing de-anchoring of inflation expectations rise. How concerned should we be? Below, we re-visit our twelve metrics to quantify perceived pressures on the US inflation anchor. We first asked, Has the Fed lost its inflation anchor?, in Feb 2022, just before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. To answer it, we built a framework from two papers by the IMF and Ricardo Reis of the LSE. It measures pressure on the inflation anchor through four gauges: the deviation of expectations from the central bank target, the variability and dispersion of those expectations, and their sensitivity to surprises. We apply them to consumers, financial markets and professional forecasters, creating a 12-point measure of anchoring and de-anchoring pressures over time. Figure 1 shows the aggregate as a rolling 10-year z-score. As of May, pressure on the inflation anchor had risen to 0.65: still above average, but only about half the April 2022 peak. In short, if the anchor is starting to loosen again, the pressure so far remains modest. That said, views differ across economic agents. Leveraged investors: Convergence dynamics in the cash futures basis is less mechanical than in a stable CTD regime. The basis trade would be exposed to CTD switches, repo assumptions, delivery timing, curve reshaping, and relative value dynamics between bonds. As market yields rise towards 6%, small shifts in these variables can trigger a switch. Liquidity premia could build around neighboring securities, given the likelihood of switches into any of them. For instance, as the liquidity premium in a CTD rises, the relative value attractiveness of delivering into another bond becomes more attractive, driving demand into those securities and lifting their liquidity premia as well. Last, as the futures duration extends in sell-offs, shorts may also need to cover. Dealers: Primary dealers hedge their long Treasury cash positions by being short futures, effectively running cash futures basis trades. Unlike hedge funds, whose motive is driven by RV/ arbitrage, the basis trade for dealers is a hedge of balance sheet exposure. records.text: Euro Area—Checking in on Inflation Expectations Inflation expectations across all horizons have shifted upwards in the Euro area following the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East and the subsequent surge in energy prices. This trend raises the question of additional upside pressure on inflation via the expectations de-anchoring channel. In this Daily, we update our summary measure for short- and long-term inflation expectations, document the recent shifts in expectations distributions and provide granular insights into the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey (CES)—a pivotal indicator of consumer inflation and broader economy perception in the region. Our “short-term” expectations series aggregates data from firms (European Commission Price Trends Survey and the ECB’s Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises, SAFE), professional forecasters (the ECB’s Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF) and Consensus Economics), consumers (the ECB’s CES), and market-based indicators (1-year zero-coupon inflation swaps). Each of these series has seen a notable increase in the readings published since the beginning of March, with our summary measure rising to its highest value since late 2023 (Exhibit 1, left). Notably, median consumer expectations for inflation over the next 12 months in CES jumped to 4% in March from 2.5% in February. According to our analysis, when superlong JGB yields rise above the upper end of their range over the past three months, foreign investors tend to be net buyers of superlong JGBs, while domestic investors tend to be net sellers ( Figure 8). In other words, volatility-averse domestic investors tend to shift into a wait-and-see stance when yields break to new highs and maintain that stance until a new range is established. records.text: system. In April, we thought this setup would lead the Fed to dial back RMPs to just $10bn/m, and that is exactly what it did last week (see here). But the softness in funding conditions is not just a function of higher reserve levels; it also reflects a meaningful increase in bank balance sheet capacity. In Q1, total leverage exposure at six of the US GSIBs expanded nearly $1trn, likely reflecting the banks' taking the option of early adoption. This represents only about a portion of the total capacity SLR changes could ultimately unlock (see here), suggesting further balance sheet expansion, and greater intermediation capacity is likely taking place this quarter. This dynamic has further eased funding conditions, effectively flattening the reserve demand curve. Y-9C data released over the past few days confirmed this early read from Q1 earnings, and show that bank balance sheets expanded $1.3trn in Q1 (and $1.9trn year-over-year). Roughly $300bn of that was in reverse repo. Securities holdings rose about $400bn, including $100bn in Treasury trading books (see the appendix for full details). Taken together, this points to a meaningful expansion in intermediation capacity across cash and repo markets, the outcome regulators were aiming for in relaxing the SLR requirement. FIGURE 1. The US and China are far ahead of Europe in diffusion, structural readiness, and adaptability, while Europe’s regulatory constraints and fragmentation risk locking it into a slower path. Small differences in diffusion speed could yield large, persistent divergences, with the US and China potentially jumping to much higher productivity trajectories as Europe lags. We nudge up headline CPI, now expecting 3.8% in April, breaching 4% by May, and peaking at 4.7% in February 2027. We expect core inflation to peak at 3.9%. Rising fuel prices also increase the risk of stronger wage demands, especially outside the public sector. We now expect two 25bp rate hikes in May and July (previously one hike), taking the policy rate to a 7.25% peak . SARB is then likely to remain o n hold until mid-2027, before easing conditions allow cuts. The near -term risk is higher fuel prices, as an input cost for farmers. Fertiliser prices remain elevated while supply is still fine. records.text: ur view. Aggregate demand surged from H1 2021 as major Western economies started to reopen in earnest from the Covid-19 pandemic, having deployed huge fiscal and monetary stimulus. Supply subsequently became increasingly problematic. China’s continued lockdown prevented production and logistics from normalizing fully, supply chains remained disrupted, ports were still dysfunctional and shipping capacity proved insufficient. As a result, prices of various goods skyrocketed as energy supplies failed to keep up. Energy prices then accelerated even higher — along with prices of wheat and other foods — following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. To summarize, global inflation pressures ended up intensifying due to a combination of (i) a sharp recovery in aggregate demand attributable at least in part to aggressive fiscal and monetary policy; (ii) supply-side disruption; and (iii) sharp rises in the price of energy, petroleum products and foods, driven predominantly by geopolitical factors. KEY MESSAGES Price hiking by Japanese firms in response to the Middle East conflict has been driven solely by energy and petroleum. Without yen depreciation or food pressures, PPI inflation is unlikely to rise as much as it did during 2021-2022. records.text: trategy: JGB vulnerability re-exposed, 20 May January 2026. JGB vulnerability is again exposed with the global rise in rates. If the rise reaccelerates, restoring market confidence will be needed as a fundamental solution, but supply-demand measures are the near term focus. We revise up our yen rates forecast, but fiscal policy remains a risk. Return of inflation risk premium The sharp global bond market sell-off has once again exposed the vulnerability of the JGB market. The global rise in rates triggered by heightened tensions in the Middle East had shown signs of pausing in April, including in the JGB market, but since last week upward pressure has again strengthened beyond the previous range, and the pace accelerated further at the start of this week. With the 30y UST yield reaching its highest level since 2007, the 30y JGB yield rose to a record high, while the 5y and 10y JGB yields also reached their highest level in 29 years ( Figure 5). Moreover, despite the rise in overseas yields taking a breather on 18 May, the JGB market continued to sell off on 19 May, only to stabilize somewhat on 20 May with the smooth passage of the 20y auction. Software comprises a larger share of US spec- grade credit today than Shale Energy did in 2016. And in private credit specifically, software & software-related names comprise a greater share of the asset class than the Telecom sector did to $HY in 2000. The ability for software to disrupt spec-grade financing conditions, for B & CCC rated credits in particular, is likely underappreciated. But there is still inertia in the overall credit ecosystem that is preventing this software stress from propagating more broadly. To us, this inertia is not necessarily a sign of strength but could simply be storing up problems for a step- function like tightening in future financial conditions. As we discuss below, the catalyst for software stress to spread will start with tangible impacts of AI disruption in software earnings, leading to a notable pick-up in software downgrades that swell the share of CCC-rated loans in loan indices & CLO portfolios, at the same time private credit funds are forced to take more meaningful markdowns on their existing software loan book. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 18 Fiscal policy presents a familiar challenge. The Treasury’s trilemma of building spending pressures, the fiscal rules, and a manifesto which inhibits capacity for large tax increases is back in focus. This is all the more salient as the headroom against the fiscal rules continues to be eroded. While the bulk of the pressure has come from the combination of higher borrowing costs and the reversal of a planned fuel duty increase (see: European Economics - Is the energy price shock derailing the fiscal impulse?), further pressures are growing. The Prime Minister has recently announced a further £18bn in defence expenditure which – while absent details such as whether this spending lands in CDEL or RDEL, and what time frame it takes place over – will add to these pressures. The Q3 and Q4 energy price caps will also be important to watch. While we think the Q3 one will pass without intervention (in part because of the fuel duty changes), the government may come under pressure to spend to shield households as we approach winter. Monetary policy still on hold. We continue to maintain that Bank Rate will be on hold at 3.75% for the remainder of 2026. This scenario implies meaningfully lower total returns across the major regions—especially in the USD IG market. The second implication, however, is much more nuanced. In our view, the drivers of the rate move matter much more for credit spread performance and investor risk appetite than the direction. For example, a move higher in nominal yields due to growth optimism is a generally supportive backdrop for corporate credit risk. While it presents a headwind for total returns, it would likely keep spreads range bound and encourage capital deployment into the credit asset class (consistent with the ‘yield-based’ bid we recently highlighted). records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 26 Czech Republic, Hungary, & Poland Czech Republic The Czech economy is forecast to grow by around 2.1% YoY this year despite the negative supply shock amid ongoing tensions in the Middle East, supported mainly by household consumption, real wage growth, and a gradual recovery in investment. The output gap should remain slightly negative this year and close only in 2027, when growth is expected to accelerate to 2.6% YoY. Headline inflation is projected at 2.4% YoY this year, driven mainly by higher energy and fuel prices and persistent core pressures in services, while temporarily overshooting 3% at the start of next year, when it should average 2.6% YoY. While a detailed breakdown is not yet available, we attribute this improvement partly to a boost in consumer demand, supported by accommodative fiscal policies and a one-off pre-election increase in public sector wages. records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 3 Philippines in Focus Jojo Gonzales ^^ Philippine Equity Partners jojo.gonzales@pep.com.ph Current account deficit seen to widen sharply Before the war in the Middle East (ME) broke out at the end of February 2026, the Philippines was on track for moderate growth, receding inflation, and narrowing twin deficits. Fast forward to May 2026 and the combo of slower GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth and higher inflation is apparent. What may be less obvious is a sharply wider current account (CA) deficit forthcoming. Pre-war, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas anticipated an improvement in the CA deficit in 2026E to US$13bn (or 3% of GDP), from US$16bn in 2025. However, with oil seen to average US$92.5/bbl in FY26E (from US$65/bbl pre-war), we believe this would widen the trade deficit, and subsequently, the CA deficit. We forecast a CA deficit in 2026E of US$21bn, or 4.1% of GDP. Exhibit 1: On track to a record CA deficit in $ terms The CA deficit to GDP is also seen to reach 4.1% in 2026E which is worse since the recent peak in 2022 at 4.5%. Risk: The primary risk we see to this trade is that the RBA holds the cash rate steady in May, potentially due to increased uncertainty in the Middle East conflict resulting from further escalation or a breakdown of current talks. This could lead some board members to adopt a more cautious approach in May, as they did in March. "1 Regardless of how the politics play out, we think oil markets are priced for the best case scenario and see risks to our $100/b forecast for Brent in 2026 skewed higher. Inventories continue to decline at a fast pace. Our global total oil inventory indicator, excluding the Middle East Gulf region to filter out the noise from the backlog of floating storage there, suggests the inventory builds in 2025 have already been more than offset (Figure 1). Adjusted for pre-pandemic seasonality (2017-19 seasonal average), the indicator stood at -60 mb last week, compared with -50 at the end of 2024 (Figure 2). However, the fundamental picture is significantly tighter, for several reasons. First, inventories are a lagged indicator for the effect of the ongoing supply disruption. Even if the Strait of Hormuz were to fully reopen today, it would take at least four weeks before the shipments from the Gulf start showing up materially in destination countries. In the past four weeks, this indicator suggests inventories have dropped by 150 mb. At this pace, the starting point for inventories even in the most optimistic scenario will be roughly 20 mb below the tightest level in recent history. records.text: US Rates Weekly 22 May 2026 Citi Research 16 Japan had a meaningful decrease in long-term UST holdings in March at $23.5bn (z-score of -1.54). While Japanese demand for long-term USTs typically decreases in March, we also do not usually see sales of this magnitude in March (Figure 30). Additionally, reserve assets data from MoF shows limited declines after accounting for the sell-off in March. So, these sales are most likely from Japanese private investors reacting to the conflict induced rates volatility in March. Official sales from China Foreign officials sold about $24bn long-term USTs (z-score of 0.7) and $12bn T- Bills in March. This brings their overall long-term UST purchases in the first quarter of this year to about $7.5bn. We do not expect demand from foreign officials to pick up anytime soon unless we get a quick resolution to the conflict in the Middle East. The US dollar has been strengthening against currencies of Asian emerging market countries like India, Indonesia and Korea (Figure 31). These countries will be forced to sell Treasuries to protect their currencies against the dollar until the conflict is resolved. So, we find it hard to expect any improvement in demand for USTs from these countries in the near term. Figure 30. While March is not a seasonally strong month for demand from Japan, $23bn of sales is not usual. Part of the decline could be official sales. Figure 31. We expect an uptick in the annual inflation of tourism-related items: Air fares and package holidays inflation dropped meaningfully last month, reflecting negative base effects from an unusually large monthly price increase last year on a late Easter dating. In May, we expect this to correct upward. Specifically for package holidays we expect a small monthly price increase with the price index returning closer to the 2025 level (Exhibit 14 ). Air fare prices should go down but not as much as last year, which drives the annual inflation rate up ( Exhibit 15 ). While these stocks strike us as likely to be sufficient for still some time, it’s admittedly unclear how low these inventory levels can safely go. records.text: 22 May 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Week in review April final HICP April headline HICP was confirmed at 3.0% YoY in the final print (2.5% in March). Core HICP was also unchanged at the 2.2% flash reading (2.29% in March). Both figures were in line with consensus. The April readings for both headline and core are broadly consistent with the ECB’s Q2 baseline forecasts of 3.1% and 2.2%, respectively. Looking at the components, higher energy HICP (up to 10.8% from 5.1% in March) drove the rise in the headline rate. Core goods too accelerated to 0.79% YoY (from 0.52% prev.) – two-tenths higher than we expected. Upward pressure came from clothing – boosted by a sharp increase in Spain – and IT equipment. Services inflation eased to 2.97% YoY (3.24% prev.), as base effects from Easter falling earlier this year weighed on the print, namely on airfares and package holidays. This drop, however, is likely to be temporary and we expect services to rebound in May. For more, see our latest Inflation Chartbook. May flash PMIs The key message emerging from May flash PMI data is a clear weakening of the economy, indicating it is firmly in a recessionary orbit. The Composite PMI for activity eased to 47.5 in May, a 1.2-pts decline from the French print. This level would typically be consistent with a quarterly GDP contraction of 0.3%. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 3 Household survey: weakness worth watching However, the Household survey was weak in April. Household employment declined by 226k, marking the fourth consecutive drop and creating a divergence from the Establishment survey’s NFP (Nonfarm Payroll) print. This divergence is not uncommon, and we typically place more weight on the Establishment survey signal, given the survey's lower standard error (~120k vs ~500k). But the Household survey signal is still worth monitoring (Exhibit 2). Also, broader slack measures showed some weakness: U6 rose to 8.2% (highest since 2021), part-time workers for economic reasons saw an increase and unemployment duration rose as well. Labor force participation edged down to 61.8%, driven by the 55+ cohort, while prime-age participation held steady, an important offset. Overall, we see the labor market as solid, but not necessarily heating up. Wages: steady, not inflationary When judging whether the labor market is becoming hot and potentially inflationary, wage dynamics are key. One metric we track closely is the wage premium for job switchers. Measures of this premium, including from our Bank of America Institute, do not suggest the labor market has tightened to start the year. Atlanta Fed data show some modest firming after the premium effectively disappeared between mid-2024 and mid-2025. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 7 Fed: labor solid enough to stay put, not hot enough to hike The April FOMC minutes are broadly consistent with our labor market outlook. Participants noted that labor market conditions are expected to remain broadly stable, with risks to employment still tilted to the downside. Admittedly, this meeting took place before the April jobs report. But in our view, the bottom line is that the FOMC is not yet ready to give the labor market an “all clear,” despite the recent improvement in the data. In turn, rate hikes are probably still a ways away. For the Fed to hike under Warsh, we think core PCE inflation would have to take another leg up (to around 3.5% or higher), and the u-rate would have to fall to 4.0% or lower. The Fed might hike sooner if wages were to accelerate or long-term inflation expectations were to unanchor, but there is no sign of that for now. The true test lies ahead Finally, while both the labor market and consumer spending have held up in the last couple of months since the start of the Iran war, the real test lies ahead. Tax refund- related tailwinds have supported consumption in recent months, even in the face of higher gas prices, particularly for higher-income households. Our base case remains that consumption growth will stay near trend. Instead, we preview the data and events of the follow week here. Money and credit (Mon – 1 June) The latest money and credit data (from which we derive the credit impulse – a leading indicator of private domestic demand) will be released on Monday (1 June). As we discussed in a blog post this week, there are mixed messages for the ECB from financial conditions. On the market-based (upstream) side, the recent rise in global bond yields have tightened financial conditions, but not significantly. The ECB will not be able to rely on market tightening to do their work for them. On the bank-based (downstream) side, lending flows and the credit impulse have remained fairly robust recently, suggesting there is scope for the ECB to tighten more if it wishes. However, the Bank Lending Survey (whose credit conditions are a leading indicator for the credit impulse) shows clear warning signs. Banks are tightening credit standards amid heightened risk, and demand is softening. That could weigh on lending in the near future. Based on the analysis, we conclude that the ECB cannot rely solely on market forces and that some "measured tightening" may be needed to achieve an appropriate policy stance. MAS’ point forecast points to core inflation around 1.7% in 2Q26, slightly above 2.5% in 3Q26, 2.2 -2.3% in 4Q26, and averaging around 2% for full year 2026. While MAS deem risks to inflation outlook as skewed to the upside, these concerns appear to be primaril y driven by supply side factors at this stage. Our base case remains for MAS to pause in July – overall tone in Apr policy statement was more dovish than we earlier thought , with risks to growth outlook seemingly greater than inflation. That said, we continue to closely monitor triggers that could prompt MAS to tighten policy further. This includes signs that (1) core inflation may stay above the historical average of 1.5-2% even into 2H27, and (2) demand -pull pressures emerging stronger and broader than currently anticipated, perhaps underpinned by fir mer growth outcomes and/or labour market resilience. We also keep an eye on potential fiscal measures in the coming months, aimed at alleviating households ’ cost of living concerns and cost pressures for small businesses. Strait transits not picking up materially Reports in the last week of an increasing volume of vessel traffic exiting the Strait of Hormuz deserves some investigation. On 14 May, Iran ian state TV reported that 30 vessels were allowed to pass the Strait since the previous night, citing an IRGC naval official. 1 On the same day, it was reported that Vitol Group was offering Iraqi Basrah crude to customers, a sign that such cargoes may have exited the G ulf.2 Then o n 20 May, t wo VLCCs carrying Iranian crude were reported to have transited the Strait bound for China.3 Recent data from Kpler, which utilizes satellite imagery to improve upon AIS data, indicates little has changed. The 7 -day average eastbound passage rate of petroleum liquids is at 1.14 mmb/d, down from 1.5 mmb/d week on week. It also shows that both the U S blockade and the IRGC resumption of restrictions have had persistent effects. While overall Strait transits have clearly fallen since 19 - April, we can also see that the ratio of non -Iranian to Iranian transits has risen. The largest share of non-Iranian transits in May have been from Iraq, followed by the UAE, Kuwait, and Qatar, while Saudi origin transits have been absent (note our last weekly reading of Saudi’s Yanbu exports averaged 3.7 mmb/d). 1 “Iran Let Over 30 Ships Through Hormuz Since Last Night ”, Bloomberg Finance LP, 14 May

More recently, political risks have risen with the chances of early elections later this year, well ahead of official timeline of Feb ’2028. Historically, MYR has often appreciated into the elections but possibility of a hung parliament could be a risk to that view . records.text: Of course, for FX, verbal intervention and actual intervention will likely remain the first line of defense. As noted above, intervention warning, and actual intervention, should continue to support the JPY ahead of the 160 line of defense versus the USD. Even so, supply-demand of FX funds for the JPY continue to face persistent JPY selling pressure from Japanese investors’ overseas investment, among other factors, meaning risks are likely to remain skewed toward JPY weakness (see JPY: Post-intervention outlook, 1 May). Stopgap measures through supply-demand support may be able to buy time but this situation differs substantially from the supply-demand-driven market selloff in the first half of last year, when rates rose alongside a marked cheapening in ASW, suggesting that supply-demand improvement alone may not bring a stable market reversal. Given the latent risk of further JPY weakness from additional BoJ purchases (and the associated cost of additional FX intervention), they are unlikely to provide a fundamental solution unless the market comes to recognize fiscal discipline and BoJ rate hikes.
