records.text: World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 47 Romania: politics not yet a downgrade trigger Mai Doan MLI (UK) Themes: government instability puts fiscal consolidation and reform at risk PSD, the largest party in the government coalition, triggered a political crisis on 20 April by withdrawing its support to the reformist/fiscal -prudent PM Bolojan. The situation is still unfolding for the formation of the next government . Near term it looks manageable from fiscal/financing side, barring any major bouts of global risk aversion. But this has long-term negative implications for reforms and fiscal consolidation outlook. The biggest/most tangible risk in the coming months is the potential loss of EU recovery funds. Prolonged political instability could slow progress to complete milestones and targets by September deadline, putting the last tranches at risk (net EUR4.2bn in grant and EUR3.5bn in loans). However, it is constructive that political parties have signaled intention to cooperate on EU funds related work to minimize any funding loss. Longer term, political uncertainty and prospects of more PSD influence in the government would undermine the fiscal path towards 3% of GDP, from c.6.5% expected this year and c.6% in 2027 (on a no policy change basis). T he negative outlook on the credit will stay, but we need to see more concrete fiscal deterioration for more tangible downgrades risks to junk. In this regard, the 2027 budget will be key. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 21 May 2026 Citi Research 18 Fiscal policy presents a familiar challenge. The Treasury’s trilemma of building spending pressures, the fiscal rules, and a manifesto which inhibits capacity for large tax increases is back in focus. This is all the more salient as the headroom against the fiscal rules continues to be eroded. While the bulk of the pressure has come from the combination of higher borrowing costs and the reversal of a planned fuel duty increase (see: European Economics - Is the energy price shock derailing the fiscal impulse?), further pressures are growing. The Prime Minister has recently announced a further £18bn in defence expenditure which – while absent details such as whether this spending lands in CDEL or RDEL, and what time frame it takes place over – will add to these pressures. The Q3 and Q4 energy price caps will also be important to watch. While we think the Q3 one will pass without intervention (in part because of the fuel duty changes), the government may come under pressure to spend to shield households as we approach winter. Monetary policy still on hold. We continue to maintain that Bank Rate will be on hold at 3.75% for the remainder of 2026. records.text: 34 World at a Glance | 21 May 2026 Thailand: Calm before the storm Pipat Luengnaruemitchai Abhay Gupta Kiatnakin Phatra Securities Merrill Lynch (Singapore) Theme: Calm before the storm Thailand's Q1 GDP was solid at 2.8% YoY — beating Q4's 2.5% and driven by a surge in investment, with gross fixed capital formation up 9.9% YoY. However, t he Q1 number is essentially a pre-war snapshot. None of the real war pressures are in the data yet. Q2 and Q3 to be where the pain arrives — weaker discretionary consumption, softer tourism spending, and potential supply disruptions if Hormuz stays closed. Fiscal relief and strong investment provide partial buffers . The Cabinet has approved an Emergency Decree authorizing the Ministry of Finance to borrow up to Bt400bn, about 2% of NGDP, to provide relief to the energy crisis and to support the energy transition. The public-debt path is expected to be closer to the self -imposed ceiling of 70% of GDP. On policy rate, we now expect no policy rate change throughout 2026. Key risks Rising oil prices beyond our baseline scenario could add pressure on inflation, fiscal position, and current account balance even further and put policy rate on hold for longer than expected. Rising global rates could put pressure on long term bond yield a nd currency depreciation which could lead to further imported inflation and create trade- offs for the BOT between higher inflation and lower growth.. While equities remain near all-time highs and interest rates elevated, the underlying relationship (on a daily or weekly basis) has rarely been as important—or as negative—as it is today (Exhibit 1). Since the start of the conflict, a 10bp move in US 10-year yields (up) has corresponded to roughly a 1.5% move (down) in the STOXX 600, while a similar move in German Bund yields has driven closer to a 2% move (down). Why are equities so sensitive to rates? 1. The Level: higher yields increase fragility. In the US, 10y yields at 4.6% are within a range (4.5–5.0%) that has historically coincided with more negative equity–rate correlations. records.text: April industrial production (29 May) We estimate that industrial production decreased -0.2% m/m in April (March revised: -0.4%), marking a third consecutive decline. As of March, METI forecast indices pointed to a decrease of -0.7% in April (index adjusted for forecasting error). In that survey, the largest negative contribution came from the inorganic and organic chemicals industry, reflecting the impact of the Middle East situation. According to METI, March was also affected by a concentration of scheduled maintenance work at naphtha crackers and other facilities. According to statistics released by the Japan Petrochemical Industry Association on 21 May, ethylene production in April rose just 3.6% m/m, indicating only a modest recovery. By contrast, polyethylene and polypropylene posted sharp recoveries from the previous month. However, all remained more than 20% below previous year’s levels. Production in this industry will remain a focus of attention going forward. 22 May 2026 18 Barclays | Market Strategy Japan: Supplementary budget and hawkish BoJ

Among countries slated to see smaller increases, several of them (including Indonesia and India) seek to stabilize domestic fuel prices. Thus, the oil shock is manifest in these cases as a deterioration in fiscal performance more than a rise in headline inflation. Even so, the clear takeaway is that higher oil prices are broadly passing through to higher inflation in many countries. T o date, the upsurge in global energy inflation remains well below that seen during the Russia-Ukraine war (Figure 11). That said, we are braced for further increases as higher petroleum prices increasingly pass-through. Also, global food inflation has remained subdued. However, supply chains for fertilizers look vulnerable, and there are also rising risks to global agricultural production from a disruptive El Niño event, which is looking increasingly likely. We forecast core inflation (i.e., excluding food and energy) for only a handful of countries (Figure 12). But the median increase is around ½ ppt, or roughly half as large the expected increase in headline inflation. Information Center, Morgan Stanley Research The area where investors expressed the most pushback during our Summit was the strategy team’s equalweight rating on the banking sector. To be sure, the banking sector appears increasingly attractive as both a direct beneficiary of rising interest rates and one of the few remaining “uncrowded trades.” However, while our Japan economics team believes the BOJ policy rate could reach 1.5% by October 2027 if inflation persists, they also see risks that further rate hikes could be delayed or paused should Middle East tensions worsen. Meanwhile, the market has already priced Japan’s terminal rate at around 2.1%, making it increasingly difficult to envision a further structural expansion in Japanese banks’ P/E multiples driven by a faster BOJ hiking cycle compared with the past. We thus maintain our equalweight stance on the banking sector.

records.text: per capita., Normalized to 100 from start Source: BofA Global Research BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH AI likely pushes r* higher for fast adopters (US/China) Countries that adopt AI rapidly —most notably the US and China — are likely to experience higher r* as sustained productivity gains lift the marginal product of capital and boost investment demand. Slower adopters — such as Europe and many EMs— are likely to see smaller r* increases, if any, as their productivity lift will be weaker. AI’s effect on r* is inherently mixed. On one side, durable productivity gains from automation, better decision‑making, and new business models raise investment demand, mirroring episodes like electrification or the late‑1990s tech boom, when firms front‑loaded capex and real rates climbed. The impact on r* could be transitory if AI only delivers a level boost to productivity, although we think it will likely be more permanent as we see AI impacting the growth rate of productivity. But several structural forces push back. If AI raises capital income more than labor income, the resulting increase in inequality may lift desired savings, as high‑income households save more, dampening consumption and offsetting investment‑driven upward pressure on r*. Roughly 10 million barrels a day of petroleum supply are currently offline, and the price of Brent oil is trading around $110/barrel. As such, we judge that the downside risks to economic activity and the upside risks to inflation remain acute. Even so, various real-time readings on global economic activity have continued to point to solid performance. This reflects the accelerating strength of AI spending. But more broadly, the global economy looks to be absorbing the oil shock fairly smoothly. Various dimensions of adjustment have been in play.1 These include a drawdown of global oil inventories and a shift to other fuel sources, as well as efforts to increase efficiency and, ultimately, “demand destruction” due to the direct effects of higher oil prices. Consistent with this view, the March and April readings of the global PMIs have held up surprisingly well (Figure 1). The services PMI has retreated a notch over this period, and it’s currently running near the lower end of its range in recent years. After combing through their 10-K & 10-Q filings, we see that any software loan markdowns taking place are very gradual and ultimately insufficient. For example, through the end of Q1’26, the median private credit software loan was still valued at a price of 98, while the 25th percentile of private credit software loans was still valued at 95.6. This is far more optimistic than what the very similar US leveraged loan market is signalling. The median US Lev Loan software name trades at 95.2, while the 25th percentile of US Lev Loan software names trades at 79.6. This inertia in private credit market pricing is quite striking in the tails of the distribution. Careful readers will just have noted the 25th percentile of private credit software names are marked with a higher valuation than the median US Leveraged Loan software name. And when we look at distress ratios, the story is similar. Only 5.8% of private credit software loans were valued at a price less than $80 at the end of Q1, compared to 25.6% of US Lev Loan software loans today that are now trading below $80. However, things have of course changed since rising costs started to cause so much stress in spring 2022, with consumers continuing to spend even as prices kept climbing. To reiterate, this was largely a reflection of households having accumulated substantial ‘excess savings’ buffers during the pandemic, partly as a result of income support and partly due to behavioral restrictions. Inflation ended u p displaying greater stamina than might otherwise have been the case as consumption accordingly held up well despite the continued price hikes. That unit profits have been rising faster than unit labor costs is clear evidence that firms have become prepared to raise their selling prices by more than what was necessary to simply cover higher wages. Households no longer have “excess savings” to rely on. However, nominal wages have continued to grow (with base-pay increases once again exceeding 3% this spring), rising stock prices have been generating positive wealth effects, and the government clearly remains inclined towards using fiscal resources to fund energy subsidies and a consumption tax cut. We no longer see rate cuts prospects from 3.75% currently, and recently revised down 2026 GDP growth forecast to 3% from just under 4% previously. High real rates and a lower inflation starting point generally allow the central bank to wait and see instead of reacting pre‑ emptively, so the bar to hike is high. Policy makers watch second round effects, rather than headlines, are the main risk. But within CEE, we see Poland as more sensitive to CPI overshooting risks – partly driven by higher gas exposure in the CPI basket and expired energy price cap schemes, more fiscal vulnerability, and a relatively less dovish central bank vs CEE peers. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 22 May 2026 11 Why do we still expect modest hikes? We still think the BoE is likely to hike twice (with risks of one) in coming months to guard against second round effects. We expect energy prices to remain high through the year (with oil close to $100) and we think this elevated shock can raise risks of second round effects, especially given above-target inflation in the past few years, consumer sensitivity to high inflation and already elevated inflation/wage expectations. Inflation is likely to pick up in coming months, and survey indicators point to elevated input/output prices, increasing risks of companies passing on costs to consumers. We would be cautious in overinterpreting the downside surprise in April services inflation/ big fall in April payrolls, given erratic components driving some of the fall. Payrolls tend to be revised often and in April revisions are normally large. Other survey indicators of labour market are showing some signs of stabilization. Moreover, the BoE is currently taking some comfort from the tightening in financial conditions weighing on inflation, but the BoE actually needs to credibly deliver on the hikes priced in to maintain those tight financial conditions. We have argued that macroeconomic uncertainty caused by higher crude oil prices and related factors, ie, the inflation risk premium, has been leading the rise in JPY IRS rates (see Macroeconomic uncertainty spilling into JPY IRS and volatility, 30 April), and the same is true of the JGB term premium. The recent JGB term premium has surged to well above the fair value implied by long-term drivers such as JGB supply-demand conditions. This upside deviation from the long-term fair value can be explained by short-term factors such as the rise in the inflation risk premium since last autumn. Figure 13 shows a decomposition of the fair value of the 10y JGB term premium into long-term factors and short-term factors, ie the inflation risk premium component, measured by the change in 10y BEI since October 2025 11 . Looking ahead, with the outlook for the Middle East situation still highly uncertain, factors related to higher crude oil prices, as seen in the sharp acceleration in the April PPI announced on 15 May, are likely to continue pushing up the inflation risk premium. In addition, as broad- based increases in goods prices begin to show up in hard data, future inflation uncertainty is likely to rise further, leaving the JGB term premium under sustained upward pressure. 22 May 2026 26

Second, this week overlaps with GSEs’ “float period,” during which MBS issuers build up cash reserves that temporarily deploy into the repo market ahead of making principal and interest payments. Third, limited carry in cash/futures bases may have led to reduced demand for leverage, with a steady reduction in levered funds’ short position (Exhibit 3). We expect some reversal of this downdraft in funding costs over the coming weeks. Bill issuance has turned positive and the Fed has reduced RMPs, any effects from the “float period” should fade, and the TGA is likely to increase to levels closer to Treasury’s target over the coming month. Even accounting for these factors, we think there is likely scope for RMPs to slow further, with our baseline for purchases to decline to a $5bn per month average until early 2027, which we expect to take the steady state level of reserves to ~11% of bank assets (versus 11.5-12.0% recently)—levels we estimate are consistent with tri-party rates settling slightly below IORB. As discussed earlier this week, there are downside risks to our Fed balance sheet projections, but we see a high bar to a meaningful decline in balance sheet size.
